title: What Nature’s Silence Said to Annie Dillard
excerpt: “Nature’s silence is its one remark,” Annie Dillard wrote in a 1981 Atlantic essay
body: “Nature’s silence is its one remark,” Annie Dillard wrote in a 1981 Atlantic essay
Dillard, who died yesterday at age 81, spent her life listening

She opens that essay, “Teaching a Stone to Talk” —which was later adapted into a collection by the same title—with the story of a man named Larry who is trying to get a rock to speak to him. “He keeps it on a shelf,” she writes, protected “by a square of untanned leather, like a canary asleep under its cloth

Larry removes the cover for the stone’s lessons.” Dillard is not sure what exactly happens at these lessons, but she respects the process: “It is a noble work, and beats, from any angle, selling shoes.” To Dillard, striving to hear the natural world was holy work too. “What have we been doing all these centuries but trying to call God back to the mountain, or, failing that, raise a peep out of anything that isn’t us?” she asks
Born in 1945 in Pittsburgh, she found inspiration in some of the places she lived
At age 28, she published Pilgrim at Tinker Creek , a Pulitzer Prize–winning nonfiction book that draws from her walks in the Blue Ridge Mountains in Virginia in the ’70s
Her musings on these solitary experiences in nature drew comparisons to Henry David Thoreau, who strongly influenced her work
She was also one of the first women to find a place in the male-dominated genre of wilderness writing

The writer Diana Saverin, who spent time going through an archive of Dillard’s personal writings and correspondence at Yale, once described in The Atlantic Dillard’s trepidation about how she would be received: “Before she published her book, she scribbled in her journal, wondering who would take her book seriously if its author was a ‘Virginia housewife named Annie.’” She dealt with this problem by leaving her day-to-day suburban life out of her work, so much so that some critics felt that she was exaggerating just how often she was in the wildness of nature

As Saverin noted, Dillard acknowledged that “she sometimes distorted the literal truth to achieve an artistic one.” But to Dillard, the ultimate truths revealed themselves in the time she did spend outside

In her journals, she acknowledged the “theological” sensibility in her books, and it is there on every page. “What is the difference between a cathedral and a physics lab?” she wrote in The Atlantic . “Are they not both saying Hello” to the world beyond? Throughout her life, Dillard identified, in turn, with Protestantism, Catholicism, and nothing at all
I first encountered her work in a religious-studies class at Wesleyan University, where she taught from 1979 to 2001, before my time there

Dillard was a shock to my system: Growing up as an observant but theologically confused Jew, I spent my teenage years in synagogue itchy with guilt, poring over the same words in the prayer book every Saturday and willing myself to believe
Only later did I come to understand that faith—and, perhaps more important, the very act of living—can also be found in what we see and touch and hear: even in the rustle of the wind

Dillard taught me this. “At a certain point you say to the woods, to the sea, to the mountains, the world, Now I am ready,” she wrote in 1981. “You feel the world’s word as a tension, a hum, a single chorused note everywhere the same
Nature does utter a peep—just this one.” Sometimes nature thunders, giving us no choice but to listen

Describing a total eclipse , Dillard is in awe, even afraid: “It was as though an enormous, loping god in the sky had reached down and slapped the Earth’s face.” Other times, nature’s peep can feel anticlimactic, but even this quiet commands reverence

The stone never does talk to Larry, and Dillard ends that story by succumbing to her faith in the nothingness. “You take a step in the right direction to pray to this silence,” she writes. “Pray without ceasing.”

title: The Most Powerful Man in AI Isn’t Worried at All
excerpt: For AI doomers, signs and portents are everywhere
body: For AI doomers, signs and portents are everywhere
When OpenAI introduced ChatGPT, almost four years ago, it couldn’t do basic arithmetic
Now the company has unreleased models that are more fluent in higher mathematics—the language of the universe—than all but the most highly trained mathematicians
If these AIs are not already the world’s best hackers, they’re very close
To plot their most audacious hacks, they’ve created makeshift message boards on the public internet
No one knows what they’ll do next—and no one can know, because the models now understand when their capacities are being tested
We’ll never again be able to say exactly how the most advanced AIs will behave unsupervised
Some of the most powerful people in AI say they are filled with dread, and are issuing statements of grave concern
On Saturday, Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, warned that self-improving AIs could soon go rogue and take over the entire internet
He called for a slowdown in AI development and promised to bring outside monitors into his company’s operations
Sam Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, quickly vowed to take similar measures
In recent weeks, both companies have seen researchers resign for fear of what they might soon create
Notably absent from the chorus of Cassandras is Jensen Huang, the CEO of the chipmaker Nvidia, the AI industry’s chief supplier of high-end semiconductors
At least twice in the past week alone, Huang has publicly dismissed existential concerns about AI as being overblown and unscientific

At a Goldman Sachs conference on September 10, he accused industry executives of fomenting cybersecurity fears to goose the market for their own products. “What better way to create demand than to create a problem?” he said
It’s a testament to Huang’s influence that he can so cavalierly mock his most important customers without fearing blowback
Neither Amodei nor Altman can afford to alienate Huang

They desperately need Nvidia’s chips to train their most advanced models, and no matter who pulls ahead in the race between them, Huang stands to gain—both on account of the chip sales and also the equity stake that Nvidia has in both companies
Even President Trump has sought favor with Huang
Trump brought Huang with him on a state visit to China earlier this year
On Monday, while Huang was onstage ripping Amodei’s doomerism at a taping of the popular tech-industry podcast All-In , Trump called his cellphone

Huang put him on speaker, and as the live audience hooted and clapped, the two men bonded over their shared view that, as Trump put it, doomerism is “all a hoax.” Huang has never evinced much concern about catastrophic risks from AI

In May of 2023, when it was becoming clear that large language models are an unusually powerful technology, more than 350 of the industry’s leaders—including Amodei and Altman—signed a statement that placed the risk of extinction from AI on the same high shelf as “other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war.” Huang didn’t sign, and neither did anyone else from Nvidia, suggesting either a remarkable conformity of opinion at the company, or perhaps something else

Later that year, he told The New Yorker that he’d never worried about the technology, not even once. “All it’s doing is processing data,” he said. “There are so many other things to worry about.” As concerns about what AI might do have circulated well beyond industry insiders, Huang’s irritation has intensified, perhaps because they represent a threat to his business. (Nvidia did not respond to my request for an interview with Huang.) He has repeatedly brushed off calls for regulation, stressing that safety is an engineering problem, not a legal one

In January, Huang said on the podcast No Priors that the “doomer narrative” is “not helpful to people, it’s not helpful to the industry, it’s not helpful to society, it’s not helpful to the governments,” and earlier this summer, he told Axios that the notion that AI would bring about the end of humanity was “complete nonsense.” In the meantime, he has repeatedly pressed Trump to lift restrictions on chip sales to China, potentially allowing AI research (and any associated risks) to proliferate on a global scale
Unlike Amodei, who regularly publishes long essays, Huang has yet to issue a manifesto defending his minority view
To understand why he remains so relaxed about AI risk, all we have to go on are stray comments
Several times over the years, he has returned to the idea that AIs will, in a sense, police their own kind

In October of 2024, he told the podcast BG2 that we can rely on AIs to monitor the most powerful models, and more recently, he said that falling AI costs will make this automated supervision easier to achieve
That AIs have already eluded their supervisors—human and otherwise—does not seem to have troubled Huang

On only one occasion—that I could find—has he allowed for the possibility that we will create an AI that is simply too powerful to be controlled. “Someday we will have god AI,” Huang said, back in January, but that day hasn’t yet arrived
Huang seems to be doing everything in his considerable power to hasten its coming.

title: This Is Your Brain on Short-Form Video
excerpt: Among the many aspects of online life accused of rotting our brains, a certain folk psychology holds that short-form video is an especially egregious driver of
body: Among the many aspects of online life accused of rotting our brains, a certain folk psychology holds that short-form video is an especially egregious driver of the decay

In an interview last month promoting his new film, in which a London couple move their tech-dependent kids to a barn without electricity, Andrew Garfield described himself as addicted to an Instagram feed full of “weird ceramics” and Japanese craftspeople. “I’ve given all of those hours to nothing,” he told Variety . “It’s genuinely enraging because we don’t have as much control over these impulses as we should.” Even Steve Chen, one of the co-founders of YouTube—home to many a recycled TikTok on its Shorts—has said that he’s wary of his kids watching too much short-form video, because of the damage it does to attention
Sometimes, when I emerge from the dark vortex of a scroll gone too long, I worry that my thoughts will permanently become as flighty as my feed
But here’s the tricky part: Very little research exists on what short-form videos are doing to the human mind

This lack of data gives cover to tech executives, who, when faced with the potentially harmful effects of their products, can cite the difficulty of establishing any one app or feature as the cause of a person’s unraveling
Short-form video in particular is a marker of how far behind cognitive research is, compared with the relentless pace of new technology
What available studies hint at so far is at least worthy of unease, and the not-knowing is only making things worse
Research on short-form videos and cognition is difficult to conduct
Studies on human subjects tend to be slow and expensive, and academics are wary of spending years investigating apps that could be irrelevant by the time their results are published
Plus, the federal government hasn’t prioritized funding research on potentially addictive behaviors, including gambling and social-media use
The industry could help fill in the gaps by funding or even leading research, especially given that American social-media platforms have exclusive and valuable data
But companies are not particularly motivated to bankroll research that could show detrimental effects of their wildly profitable products
So far, they have largely chosen to keep internal research private. (Data points do creep out

In 2024, for instance, a sloppily redacted complaint in a lawsuit against TikTok revealed some of the company’s internal research, which allegedly found that compulsive usage of the app “correlates with a slew of negative mental health effects like loss of analytical skills, memory formation, contextual thinking, conversational depth, empathy, and increased anxiety.” At the time, a spokesperson for TikTok argued that the documents were outdated and that the quotes in the complaint had been cherry-picked.) Complicating things further is the fact that much of the publicly available research on short-form video is flimsy
In a study conducted at China’s Zhejiang University that went viral last month, 56 young adults clicked through a series of short videos (not on social media) as they lay in an MRI machine

Two brain regions involved in executing cognitively demanding tasks were found to be more active when participants swiped away from videos before they were midway through, versus when they stuck around until a video’s end
Prominent social-media accounts, including one for the prediction market Polymarket, promoted the study as more proof that TikTok is making us smooth-brained

One news outlet ran the headline “ Instagram Reels & TikTok Make You Dumb & Depressed .” But the study, multiple neuroscientists told me, said nothing about short-form videos, intelligence, or depression—instead, it found that brain areas involved in taking action lit up when a participant chose to take the action of skipping to the next video

Besides, the study lacked controls, equated finishing a video with enjoying it, and never established the baseline that supposedly video-addled brain activity was being compared against. (The study’s corresponding author did not respond to a request for comment.) Stronger studies are much rarer

But they do point in the same direction as many Americans’ intuition: Increased short-form-video use appears to be associated with poorer impulse control, mental-health outcomes, and attention capacity

Researchers at the University of Bristol concluded last year that the constant context-switching inherent to watching short-form videos may degrade prospective memory: the ability to recall something you had previously intended to do

Caty Enders, a doctoral student at the University of New Mexico, has also found that students who used TikTok at a high volume had more issues with both working memory (the information you need to keep track of what you’re doing in the moment) and episodic memory (a form of long-term memory that stores past personal events, such as what you did for your tenth birthday)

A 2024 study conducted at Sigmund Freud University, in Austria, found that participants who reported watching more than four hours of short-form videos a day exhibited neurological activity that indicates cognitive abnormality
Take all these findings with a grain of salt, however
Even the highest-quality studies on short-form videos tend to be limited in their explanatory power

And Keith Robert Head, a researcher at Capella University who recently published a review article on short-form video and attention, could point me to just four good studies on the topic that had been conducted in the United States

Most of the existing research comes from China, and Enders cautioned me against applying findings across the two countries, given that social-media platforms in the U.S. are subject to much less government control and are capable of accessing more user data and personalizing feeds to a greater degree

Psychologists and neuroscientists have reasoned that short-form video is probably an especially potent and dangerous type of social media because the constant stream of non sequiturs and bright visuals is so overstimulating, and because there’s no upper limit to how long you can spend scrolling

But no one has established whether the negative effects of short-form video are because of something specific to the medium or the fact that spending hours on TikTok displaces healthy habits such as sleeping—in which case, the videos would be no more inherently harmful than binging Friends
Participants in a study Enders conducted on TikTok use and memory spent an average of 133 minutes a day on the app. “If you do anything every day for 133 minutes, it will change you,” Enders said
Uncertainty around any technology’s effects not only relieves pressure on tech companies to make targeted modifications but also leaves governments to decide policy without sufficient information
Some countries have already instituted blanket social-media bans for minors based on imperfect data —not an ideal basis on which to restrict civil liberties
And everyone else is left with the ambient and unsure sense that the apps they use are terrible for them
The fact that so many people perceive a problem with short-form video may be reason enough for alarm

Luiz Pessoa, a neuroscientist at the University of Maryland who spoke with me about the shortcomings of the recent viral study, thinks that an attention epidemic is clearly at hand, despite scientists’ limited understanding of it

He and his teenage daughter often watch the highlight reels from Formula 1 races, and when they do, she’s also looking at her phone. “It’s obvious we’re multi-, triple-, quadruple-tasking in ways that at least 20, 30 years ago we weren’t,” he told me
You don’t have to be a neuroscientist to have reason to suspect your brain can be stretched only so thin.

title: The Atrocities That Shaped the Modern Middle East
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube On this week’s episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic ’s David Frum opens with a discussion of the see
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube On this week’s episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic ’s David Frum opens with a discussion of the seemingly forgotten attack on the Yazidi people by ISIS in 2014
Then, David is joined by the historian Simon Sebag Montefiore to discuss his new book, The Cauldron: The Making of the Modern Middle East
David and Simon discuss how much of the present-day Middle East emerged from the ruins of the Ottoman empire and the violence that took place both before and after the empire’s collapse
David and Simon discuss how, one after another, different language groups and religious groups were pushed into exile or eliminated altogether
Then, David finishes with a discussion of The Hidden Hand : The Information War and the Rise of Antisemitic Propaganda, by Warren Kinsella

The following is a transcript of the episode: Simon Sebag Montefiore: So, again and again, we have this pattern where if you don’t have a state, you’re nothing, and if you do have a state, the only way to enforce it is with autocracy or with repression
David Frum: Hello, and welcome to The David Frum Show
I’m David Frum, a staff writer at The Atlantic
My guest this week will be Simon Sebag Montefiore, the acclaimed British historian and author of the new book The Cauldron: The Making of the Modern Middle East
The book discussion at the end of the show will feature The Hidden Hand by Warren Kinsella, subtitled The Information War and the Rise of Antisemitic Propaganda
But before either the dialogue with Simon Sebag Montefiore or the book discussion of The Hidden Hand , some opening thoughts on themes that will run all their way through today’s program
Simon Sebag’s book The Cauldron describes the transformation of the Middle East from its existence under the Ottoman empire a century and a half ago to the region of today, divided among many nations

And yet while the map of the Middle East is much more tangled than it was when the Ottomans ruled almost everything from Tunisia to Iraq—although parts of it were under foreign influence: British and French colonial rule, Italian colonial rule—a simple map, but with a complex reality
Simon Sebag describes how, one after another, different language groups, different religious groups, different groups with different histories were pushed into exile or eliminated altogether
I want to showcase just one of those acts of elimination to drive home what it is that we are talking about when we talk about the making of the modern Middle East
In August 2014, fighters of the Islamic terror group ISIS attacked the Yazidi minority in northwest Iraq
The Yazidis are a very ancient people who follow a pre-Islamic religion
There are about 600,000 of them living in northwest Iraq in August 2014

ISIS murdered some 3,000 to 5,000 of them , mostly men and older women, and captured 6,800 women and girls and turned them into sexual slaves for ISIS fighters, and spared the lives of some of the very young boys in order to recruit them and brainwash them as child soldiers fighting for ISIS
Religious and cultural sites belonging to the Yazidi people were systematically destroyed, and civilian infrastructure, especially water supplies, wrecked
Four hundred thousand of the 600,000 Yazidi were driven into exile, and few of those people have ever returned to their homes
Their goal was to eliminate the Yazidi people, because ISIS hated their religious traditions
ISIS condemned the non-Islamic Yazidi as devil worshipers and thought that because of their non-Islamic views, they should cease to exist as a people and even as human beings
People in the West were aware of the Yazidi genocide, and some of the Yazidi were given refuge, especially in Europe
But as time has passed, the story has faded from memory
You certainly don’t see the kind of big marches in Western countries by progressive people or other kinds of people that you’ve seen in, for example, the war that Hamas started in October of 2023

And I think the reason why we have a hard time holding onto it is because a lot of people who study the Middle East, especially the progressive-minded, have a kind of vision of how the Middle East should be

It’s a vision in which Arab nationalism and Islamic identity are seen as progressive, in the most literal sense—the trend of the future—and everything else is seen as kind of backward looking, and it shouldn’t be there
And so as Christian populations were either eliminated by force or driven into exile—as Simon and I will discuss, there were massacres of the Assyrian Christian population in Iraq
Much of the Christian population of Egypt has been driven into exile
The Armenians were the victim of two waves of genocide in Ottoman empire, one in the 1890s and again in the 1910s
The Kurds were subjected to murderous attack by Saddam Hussein’s Iraq and by the Iranian regime, too

And of course, there is the story of the Jews, who inhabited ancient communities in places like Alexandria and Baghdad, communities that existed before the coming of either the Arabs or of Islam to the region

And after 1945, those communities—or after 1941 in the Iraqi case—those communities were murdered, massacred, plundered, driven into exile, ceased to exist, in-gathered into the state of Israel, where the Jews who formerly lived all through the Ottoman empire have found refuge in one place
This great system of simplification was at every turn marked by atrocity, attempted genocide, the refusal of difference within the context of the Middle East
We don’t seem to find that so troubling because we have an implicit idea of who should be on top and who should not be on top
And this implicit understanding may, I think, add some context to why false accusations against Israel and the Jews have gained so much hearing
Because in a way, the Jews and the state of Israel stand out as the great exception to the trend of the Middle East
This is the one place—the one place—where a people that were a minority people under the old Ottoman empire have built a successful state that is able to be self-sufficient

And that exception to the trend everywhere else in the Middle East is seen by many as a kind of denial of the logic of history, which calls for the whole region to become all one thing under one language—or two, Turkish and Arabic—under one faith, Islam, everyone else driven to the wall

title: The Knives Are Out for Bill Belichick
excerpt: Ever since Bill Belichick, that aging football Caesar, arrived at the University of North Carolina roughly two years ago with his eight Super Bowl rings, the kn
body: Ever since Bill Belichick, that aging football Caesar, arrived at the University of North Carolina roughly two years ago with his eight Super Bowl rings, the knives have been out

He is one of the greatest coaches in NFL history, but his hiring was controversial: Despite no experience leading a college team, he was given a five-year, $50 million contract—$30 million of it guaranteed—to vitalize a dowdy old southern program and lift it to championship level

From the beginning, he has been fighting a two-front battle: one on the field, and another against internal opponents, a contingent of powerful Carolina traditionalists who never wanted him there, resent his outsize presence, and wish UNC to remain a quaint, basketball-first school. “It is an internal civil war,” John Preyer, the former chair of UNC’s board of trustees, who helped hire Belichick, told me
For several weeks now, Belichick’s program has been the subject of a messy, reputation-threatening internal investigation, even as his team shows promising signs in early competition
On August 5, UNC announced that it had hired outside attorneys to help with an evaluation of a personnel complaint against Belichick’s general manager, Michael Lombardi
That has since grown into a sprawling, open-ended probe of Belichick’s entire office culture, with unsavory lines of questioning
One person interviewed by the lawyers who asked not to be named for fear of retaliation told me they were asked whether they thought anyone drank on the job

The person said they were also asked about staffers’ sexual relationships, and about possible drug use by Belichick’s son Steve, who serves as his defensive coordinator but is currently on indefinite medical leave for unstated reasons. (I was not able to reach Steve Belichick for comment.) His father said at a press conference last week, “I love all my kids but I’m not going to comment on a medical situation.” [ Read: The quiet desperation of Tom Brady ] Lombardi, whose attorney has denied that his client committed any wrongdoing, resigned on September 3, but the university announced that the investigation would continue anyway

What the school did not announce was that two of the attorneys engaged by the university to investigate Belichick’s program, Nate Huff and McNair Nichols, are the subjects of whistleblower complaints over a separate investigation into the university’s School of Civic Life and Leadership (SCiLL)

In that matter, two faculty members have accused university leadership of using the lawyers as company men rather than impartial evaluators, and of tailoring the investigation’s scope, despite promising an “independent review.” According to billing documents from the SCiLL investigation that I obtained, Huff and Nichols took “instructions” from top UNC administrators. “Review strategy in light of instructions from client,” one billing memo read
Another read, “Develop new investigation timeline and strategy to comply with client instructions.” Eventually, the lawyers produced a 400-page report that UNC then refused to make public
Internal investigations are not unusual, of course
All kinds of institutions conduct them into a wide array of personnel scandals—real and perceived—all of the time
Yet multiple people at UNC told me that there is reason to doubt the intentions and objectivity of the Belichick inquiry

Dustin Sebell, a SCiLL professor of the history of political thought who has filed a formal wrongful-conduct complaint with the university over the SCiLL investigation, told me in an email that the Belichick probe has an “eerie similarity” to what he experienced

Sebell said that he participated in the SCiLL investigation based on assurances from university administrators about its independence and objectivity —assurances, he wrote in his complaint, that turned out to be “false.” Another SCiLL faculty member has filed a complaint on similar grounds

When I asked Sebell whether he thinks Belichick can expect a fair and independent review, he responded, “If history is any guide, the University is now asking for a trust it forfeited the last time around.” UNC’s vice chancellor for communications, Dean Stoyer, told me of the Belichick investigation, “I can confidently say that it has been managed independently

I can tell you that it is thorough and ongoing.” Huff replied to questions about his and Nichols’s independence by saying, “We cannot discuss any of the work we do for our clients.” Belichick was hired in 2024 over the objections of the athletic director at the time, Bubba Cunningham, who favored younger, likely cheaper, candidates
Cunningham was overruled by Chancellor Lee Roberts and members of a search committee who wanted an electrifying hire to uplift a football program that had long been an also-ran

Cunningham, an eminence who served as the chair of the NCAA men’s basketball-tournament selection committee, has since stepped down as athletic director, but he remains a powerful figure on campus, with the title of senior adviser to the chancellor and athletic director
Although he outwardly accepted Belichick’s hiring, several people told me that he has never been happy about it
Neither have others who see Belichick as encroaching on their personal power or resources
Cunningham did not respond to a request for comment. [ Read: The man who broke physics ] For 24 seasons with the New England Patriots, Belichick exercised dictatorial control
In his negotiations with Carolina, he extracted promises of autonomy over his program and more money for acquiring players and paying staff salaries

Around the time Belichick was hired, the school also said it would i ncrease its spending on football by millions, upgrade its football facilities, and build a virtual-reality training system for quarterbacks

This has been a threat to old-guard donors who feel disenfranchised, and others who want Carolina to remain focused on basketball, in the tradition built by Dean Smith—the late, legendary basketball coach with a reputation for modest virtue. “Dean is Banquo’s ghost,” Preyer told me, summoning Macbeth —a spirit haunting the athletic department
It didn’t help that Belichick’s first season ended with just four wins in 12 games, and that his personal life has regularly been in the tabloids
It is possible that Belichick presides over an unruly office that requires broad scrutiny, and that real wrongdoing has taken place
But his football team looks improved this season thanks in part to the way he’s instilled in his players a quality he’s well-known for: discipline
A team that lost by 34 points to Texas Christian University last year beat the same opponent in this year’s opener 15–10 with a superbly controlled display
The team won again on Saturday, 35–3, against East Tennessee State University

But its real test lies in the coming weeks, as it enters Athletic Coast Conference play, with games against Clemson, Notre Dame, and Miami—of which the latter two are ranked in the top five nationally

Asked last week in a press conference if he is in “control” of his program—much of his time with reporters was consumed by questions about the investigation—Belichick answered curtly in the affirmative: “If you’re around here every day, I think you’d see it.” He also said, “We want to run the program in the very best way

And if there’s things we need to do to correct it, then we’ll obviously do them.” One source with knowledge of the inquiry who asked not to be named because of their position with the university told me that Lombardi was found to have made a handful of minor NCAA-rules violations
One example: allowing recruits to have their picture taken on the field

The source said that taken as a whole, the violations were “not of the nature that would necessitate firing”—but Lombardi, a brusque New Jersey native, had alienated high-dollar donors and athletic-department officials with his way of getting things done

A friend and longtime associate of Belichick’s, Lombardi had been earning $1.5 million a year at UNC, making him the highest-paid general manager in college football, despite not having worked in college athletics since 1984. [ Read: Fifty years after history’s most brutal boxing match ] Stoyer, the UNC vice chancellor for communications, did not elaborate on the state of the investigation, or when it might conclude
Through a spokesperson, Belichick declined my requests for comment
For the time being, he will continue coaching under an ugly cloud
Last week the local Raleigh TV station WRAL reported that one line of questions had to do with whether a woman on the recruiting staff had a relationship with a player

title: Pennsylvania’s Measles Outbreak Is Enormous
excerpt: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter
body: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter
Following America’s recent measles deaths, anti-vaccine activists have cast doubt on the virus as the culprit
They’ve pointed to a victim’s underlying health conditions or, as they did last year in Texas, blamed hospital error
But the two latest measles deaths in Pennsylvania—bringing the state’s total to four since mid-August—have made the United States’ measles crisis undeniable
Last month, the Pennsylvania Department of Health announced two measles-associated deaths; both cases were later revealed to be infants too young to have been vaccinated

Kennedy Jr.—who was an anti-vaccine activist for decades before becoming health secretary—wrote on X that the deaths might have been “altogether fabricated.” (He later acknowledged a coroner’s conclusion that one of the deaths had been caused by measles.) Then, last weekend, an unvaccinated 40-year-old woman died in Jefferson County; immediately, people on Reddit and X insisted that her death wasn’t really caused by measles, because she’d had asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, both of which can make breathing difficult
Yesterday, state officials revealed that an unvaccinated 18-year-old died from a rare inflammatory condition of the brain and spinal cord that can be triggered by measles
Some commenters online deemed that death suspicious too
What the armchair epidemiologists miss is that vulnerability to the infection doesn’t make a death less real
The two infants both tested positive for measles

The Lancaster County coroner’s office determined that one infant died of a ruptured spleen; however, when I spoke with that child’s parents , they told me that the mother had been extremely ill with the disease when she gave birth, the baby was not breathing when he was born, and they believed measles had killed their son
The other infant was born with a rare neurological condition, but the coroner found that measles was ultimately the cause of death

Greg Furlong, the Jefferson County coroner who investigated the 40-year-old woman’s death, told me that although the woman had conditions that made her vulnerable to measles, and was on supplemental oxygen, she was active before she contracted the virus
She cooked for her family and cleaned the house

Measles killed her in about a week. “If she wouldn’t have got the measles, would she still be alive today? I say yes,” Furlong, a Republican who is also the mayor of Summerville, said. [ Read: The measles-stricken mother who lost her newborn son ] Four deaths in roughly four weeks suggest that the state is in the midst of an enormous outbreak
The Pennsylvania health department lists total cases at 693, with 99 in the past week
But considering that measles kills about one to three of every 1,000 children it infects, the actual number is likely much larger

Many who fall ill, particularly in the Amish community, aren’t getting tested; the Amish parents of the infant who died with a ruptured spleen told me that their 13 living children had all caught the virus, but they never got swabbed
These deaths are occurring after three unvaccinated people, including two young girls, died of measles in Texas and New Mexico last year
Those were the first measles deaths in the country in a decade
The last time the United States experienced four measles deaths in a calendar year was in 1992, at the tail end of a years-long outbreak that killed more than 100 Americans
That resurgence led to a recommendation that children receive two doses of the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine, and prompted a nationwide push to increase vaccination rates
It worked, and measles was declared eliminated in the United States in 2000

But overall kindergarten vaccination rates started declining during the coronavirus pandemic, and some areas, including Lancaster County, have fallen well below the 95 percent needed to maintain herd immunity
Now, in the face of a new increase in measles deaths, Kennedy appears more interested in scoring political points than boosting national vaccination rates

He has accused Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, of “the weaponization of infectious disease fears for political gain”; Shapiro, in turn, charged Kennedy with “playing games with public health” after the CDC declined to update its measles statistics to include the deaths in his state

Kennedy’s stated reason for the omission is that the agency is “applying a consistent national standard.” But the delay marks a shift in policy: Last year, the CDC counted both Texas girls’ deaths and the death of the adult in New Mexico after the states announced them. (In a post on X, Kennedy wrote that the National Center for Health Statistics will determine if measles is the true cause of the deaths in Pennsylvania after examining death records; a spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services did not respond to questions about that investigation

In a statement, Pennsylvania’s health department said that its investigation had determined that all four deaths met the criteria for measles-associated fatalities.) Tomorrow, Kennedy is scheduled to be the keynote speaker at the annual conference for Children’s Health Defense, the anti-vaccine organization that he founded before becoming health secretary
Children’s Health Defense has a long history of ginning up fears about the vaccine for measles, mumps, and rubella while downplaying the seriousness of the diseases

In July 2021, Kennedy told attendees at an Amish country fair in Pennsylvania, “The cure for measles is chicken soup and vitamin A.” In fact, no known cure for measles exists; vitamin A has shown some promise in people with severe vitamin A deficiency, which is exceedingly rare in the United States

Since becoming health secretary, he has stated publicly that vaccination is “the most effective way to prevent measles infection,” but as I’ve reported , he also undercut that message by telling the father of a girl who died in West Texas that “you don’t know what’s in the vaccine anymore.” Kennedy has been a stronger advocate for measles itself, which he’s falsely credited with boosting resistance to cancer and cardiac disease, than he has for the vaccine that prevents it. [ Read: What RFK Jr. told grieving Texas families about the measles vaccine ] As cases and deaths rise, the reality becomes harder to ignore: Measles, a disease the country seemingly overcame 30 years ago, is once again killing Americans.

title: Meet a mouse whose brain cortex is made up of human cells
excerpt: Human brain cells, mouse body: Scientists have grown human brain tissue inside mice, creating a hybrid creature whose cortex is largely made of human cells
body: Human brain cells, mouse body: Scientists have grown human brain tissue inside mice, creating a hybrid creature whose cortex is largely made of human cells
Why it matters: The research could unlock new ways to study brain injuries

Ethical questions loom: Mixing human brain tissue with animals raises uncomfortable questions about what it means to be human. " data-chronoton-post-id="1144210" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Multiple cameras tracked a mouse as it wandered around a small arena
A computer charted its position and speed, leaving Pong-like traces on a monitor.  The reason to watch this rodent so carefully? Nearly half its brain volume had been replaced with human cells

The effort to mix the brain tissues of distant species is being reported today in the journal Nature by a team at Stanford University, led by neuroscientist Sergiu Pașca.  Pașca’s group previously showed that human brain “organoids”—small blobs of neural tissue—could survive, and even function, after being injected into the heads of baby rodents
Now, Pașca has taken things a step further by genetically modifying mice so their brains don’t fully develop in the first place
These modified mice are missing most cells of both the cortex and the hippocampus, two key brain areas

That creates much more room for the human cells to take hold, he says. “Human cells that are placed in these animals will divide, will grow, and within a few weeks to a few months they will take most of that space,” he says
Pașca says one surprising discovery is that the mice lacking brain tissue seemed fairly normal—they walked around and squeaked
In a maze test, they couldn’t remember what parts they’d explored.  The mice with the added human cells, by contrast, performed better on the maze test
That means the human tissue is playing some role in the animals’ cognition
Pașca believes what he is calling “xenocortical mice” could be useful in studying brain injuries

However, the report is also a dramatic demonstration of “the combined power of genetic engineering and stem-cell technology to reshape biology,” says Carsten Charlesworth, a scientist who works in a different Stanford lab and was not involved in the research
Already, brain organoids are being tested in labs to see if they can be connected to computers to play video games

Other scientists have proposed using them like replacement parts to treat stroke victims.  “What’s most remarkable to me is the extent to which human neural tissue introduced after birth grew and connected with the mouse nervous system across a species barrier,” says Charlesworth. “As these technologies advance, they’ll increasingly force us to challenge our traditional assumptions.” Last year, Pașca convened a group of ethics experts to study the implications of neural organoid technology, including the odds that an animal could develop human consciousness and the risk that “organoid therapy clinics” might offer scam treatments to desperate patients
For now, he says, he’s not concerned that the rodents have any type of human cognitive capacities

That is because their brains are relatively tiny and the evolutionary distance between man and mouse is so great.  But that’s also why Pașca says this type of experiment should not be carried out on higher species: They could end up with large volumes of functioning human brain tissue, potentially blurring the cognitive boundaries between people and animals.  Pașca specifically cautioned against adding human brain organoids to a monkey engineered to lack a cortex. “One of the things that I see as a very clear red line is doing this experiment in a primate,” he says. “I don’t think that is justified at this point in any way.”

title: Building the materials foundation for AI
excerpt: The AI boom is becoming a materials challenge
body: The AI boom is becoming a materials challenge
As AI pushes computing into new territory, the materials behind that infrastructure are becoming just as crucial as the algorithms running on it

Semiconductors and data centers are approaching physical limits around performance, thermal management, electrical efficiency, and reliability, creating new demands for materials that can do more at once
At the same time, AI is giving materials scientists new ways to search the enormous universe of possible molecules and accelerate the development of solutions

For Mike Finelli, chief technology and innovation officer and chief North America officer at Syensqo, that convergence is transforming what advanced materials can enable. “AI is now, from a material standpoint, really pushing semiconductors and the data centers to their physical limits,” he says

As requirements accumulate, including high temperature, purity, electrical performance, chemical resistance, plasma resistance, and long-term stability, materials move toward what Finelli calls the “top of the pyramid.” Beyond supporting AI innovation, he contends that advanced materials are “actually increasingly defining what’s going to be possible.” That challenge is playing out across the infrastructure powering the AI surge

Syensqo is developing materials for high-voltage data center architectures, advanced sealing materials for semiconductor manufacturing, and thermal-management solutions including fluids for direct immersion cooling
Some of those innovations can also cross industry boundaries
Materials developed for electric vehicles, for example, can help address the higher voltage and energy-density demands that are emerging in data centers
The definition of performance is also changing
More customers are expecting materials to meet technical requirements while reducing environmental impact. “Our goal is to remove the trade-off between performance and sustainability,” Finelli says
That means considering sustainability at the beginning of the research process instead of treating it as an additional requirement once a material has been developed
AI is changing how those materials are discovered, too

Syensqo is using AI agents to digitally synthesize millions of potential molecular combinations, predict their performance and sustainability characteristics, and narrow them to a much smaller group for laboratory testing
The result, Finelli says, is the ability to go “broader, deeper, and faster” while giving scientists more time to solve complex engineering problems

Looking to the future, Finelli sees the possibility of a reinforcing cycle: AI helps develop materials that improve AI infrastructure, which in turn enables better AI to accelerate materials discovery

That feedback loop could create a cycle of innovation and expand what future technologies can achieve. “You end up in this accelerated materials, innovative cycle of materials innovation,” says Finelli. “That really excites me, and it gives us the opportunity to continue enabling technologies that will shape the future.” This episode of Business Lab is produced in partnership with Syensqo

Full Transcript: Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I’m Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace
This episode is produced in partnership with Syensqo

Now asked to name the key enablers to AI advancement, many of us might list algorithms, data centers, or even computing power, but just as critical to the performance are the advanced materials that underpin each layer of that innovation
As AI continues to evolve, it’s pushing the likes of semiconductors and data centers to new physical limits, putting new pressure on the advanced material sector to keep pace
As the sector rises to this challenge, AI is also emerging as a powerful tool for accelerating materials discovery and development, significantly shortening development timelines for new solutions
My guest today is Mike Finelli, chief technology and innovation officer and chief North America officer at Syensqo
Mike, can I start by asking you to tell us a little bit more about Syensqo and the role it plays in developing advanced materials? Mike: Yeah, absolutely
Syensqo is a global leader in specialty materials
Our job is to help customers solve their toughest technology challenges
We serve a lot of different markets, but the way I like to say it simply is if it flies, we’re on it
In healthcare, our products literally are saving lives every day
And if you like your mobile devices, if you like AI, it’s our products that are actually enabling the advanced semiconductor chips that are required to produce all of this
Our role is to enable innovation through advanced chemistry
We develop materials that deliver higher performances, greater reliability, and increasingly more sustainable solutions
The way I would say this, it’s at the heart of our business
Actually, it’s in our name, Syensqo

And to put some numbers around it, 20% of our annual revenues come from new products and applications that we’ve launched in the last five years, which is really evidence of a really strong innovation engine
And as you sort of described there, you’re in all sorts of different industries with an emphasis perhaps on electronics and semiconductors
Can you talk a bit more about that work and where those industries are headed perhaps? Mike: Sure
So look, electronics and semiconductors have been strategic markets for Syensqo for literally decades
I don’t want to date myself, but 33 years ago when I started in the company, semiconductors were one of the first industries that I worked in
And we’ve supported successive waves of innovation from enabling smaller, more powerful mobile devices, helping the industry get to the smaller and smaller profiles and the chips
We’ve helped to advance hyperconnectivity, supporting increasingly sophisticated semiconductor manufacturing

title: The Download: AI’s trillion-dollar gamble and OpenAI’s biology data bid
excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology

What’s at stake in AI’s trillion-dollar gamble When Jessica Wachter, a finance professor at the University of Pennsylvania, wanted to assess AI’s impact on the economy over the next few years, she faced a long list of uncertainties
So she started with a “remarkable fact” that is not in question: a handful of so-called hyperscalers are investing huge amounts of money to build AI data centers

Instead of trying to predict how widely deployed AI models will be, Wachter asked how fast the hyperscalers’ earnings will need to grow to justify their spending through 2027, when expenditures are expected to reach nearly $1.1 trillion
AI companies will need to achieve an extraordinary increase in productivity just to break even by 2030

Take a closer look at what it will take for the AI buildout to pay off. —David Rotman AI models need more data about biology, and OpenAI is paying to create it AI needs much more information to make important breakthroughs in curing disease
So last year Ruxandra Teslo, a policy analyst, posted an idea for supercharging medical AI systems: use data from failed biotech companies

By bidding at bankruptcy proceedings, she argued, it might be possible to obtain detailed regulatory filings, manufacturing strategies and safety data, creating what she called “biotech’s lost archive.”  The OpenAI Foundation, the nonprofit parent of OpenAI, announced this week that it will fund her idea, paying to create “high-quality scientific datasets.” Learn more about their new effort . —Antonio Regalado Our Roundables on AI’s extinction threat is now available on demand As frontier models become more capable, warnings about AI extinction have become widespread in Silicon Valley

But are the threats really as dangerous as they’re presented? In the latest MIT Technology Review Roundtable, executive editor Niall Firth, senior AI editor Will Douglas Heaven and AI reporter Grace Huckins took a closer look at the arguments behind those warnings
They discussed what AI extinction could actually mean, how seriously we should take the risks and what, if anything, can be done to reduce them
Subscribers can now watch an exclusive recording of the discussion

Conboy now says she has found a combination of two existing drugs that can produce youthful effects without the need for any bodily fluid exchange

One more thing Why Trump’s “golden dome” missile defense idea is another ripped straight from the movies In 1940, a fresh-faced Ronald Reagan starred in Murder in the Air , a movie centered on a “superweapon” that could stop enemy aircraft

More than 40 years later, the concept became a real-life centerpiece of Reagan’s presidency with the Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI), better known as “Star Wars.” Now Donald Trump has revived the dream
In 2024, Trump announced plans to build the “Golden Dome,” a system of sensors and interceptors on the ground, in the air and in space
It’s often compared to SDI for its futuristic sheen, its aggressive form of protection and the idea that an impenetrable shield is the cheat code to global peace

title: US consumers and businesses are now facing a future of more expensive borrowing
url:
<title>US consumers and businesses are now facing a future of more expensive borrowing</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760267/original/file-20260916-50-c1jn4i.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C4960%2C3306&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh has recently emphasized the importance of bringing inflation back down to its target of 2%.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/home/search?query=kevin%20warsh&amp;mediaType=photo">AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>From mortgages to auto loans to credit cards, borrowing is set to get even pricier.</p>

<p>But the <a href="https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20260916a.htm">Federal Reserve’s decision</a> on Sept. 16, 2026, to hike its baseline interest rate also highlighted an increasingly confounding dilemma: It can raise the price of money across the economy, but it can’t determine which sectors are most affected. </p>

<p>That means the rate increase may further slow the weaker parts of the economy, <a href="https://www.wsj.com/economy/housing/the-stagnant-housing-market-is-about-to-face-a-7-mortgage-55a041d6">such as housing</a>, while barely affecting the strongest, namely the <a href="https://www.wsj.com/finance/investing/the-quarter-trillion-dollar-onslaught-of-ai-bonds-is-testing-investors-limits-e4cd2bda?mod=article_inline">relentless investment</a> in artificial intelligence.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20260916a.htm">In its statement summarizing its unanimous vote</a>, the Fed’s policymaking committee said it was raising its benchmark rate by a quarter percentage point so that it now stands at a new target range of 3.75% to 4%. It described inflation as still “elevated” and noted that other economic indicators remain strong, from productivity to investment, to domestic spending.</p>

<p>As a <a href="https://www.bakerinstitute.org/expert/john-w-diamond?f%5B0%5D=type%3A891">scholar of public finance</a>, I believe the Fed probably had little choice but to raise rates given its commitment to maintain inflation-fighting credibility. <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/16/business/economy/federal-reserve-interest-rates-warsh.html">Markets had already expected</a> the hike, and if the Fed had failed to deliver, it might have pushed longer-term interest rates even higher amid concerns it was becoming less wedded to that target.</p>

<p>But the Fed’s action also underscores that the U.S. increasingly looks like an economy moving at two very different speeds. Investment in AI – whether through data centers, computing capacity or related infrastructure – has been booming, while it’s <a href="https://www.minneapolisfed.org/article/2026/how-is-ai-influencing-interest-rates-investment-productivity-prices-and-more">crowding out</a> other kinds of investment. </p>

<p>Meanwhile, the housing market is getting crushed by <a href="https://www.wsj.com/finance/investing/home-prices-overvalued-housing-market-4f8be55b">high mortgage rates</a> and diminishing affordability, while consumers are carrying ever more expensive <a href="https://www.wsj.com/personal-finance/credit/us-credit-card-debt-af5c7c77">credit card and auto debt</a>. </p>

<p>Many small and traditional businesses are also <a href="https://www.bankrate.com/loans/small-business/small-business-owners-are-seeking-smaller-loans/">in a bind</a> as they face substantially higher financing costs than they did several years ago. Those costs reflect the rising yields on longer-term U.S. government debt, which have been going up for months on a <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/article/treasury-bonds-yields-economy.html">mix of factors</a>: Longer-term inflation concerns due to soaring U.S. government debt, geopolitical risks driving up energy costs, and ongoing financing demand for AI. </p>

<p>On Sept. 14, the yield on the <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/14/business/10-year-treasury-yield-5-percent.html">10-year Treasury crossed 5%</a> for the first time since 2023.</p>

<h2>An elusive inflation target</h2>

<p>When the Fed hikes short-term interest rates, it <a href="https://www.federalreserve.gov/aboutthefed/fedexplained/monetary-policy.htm">slows down economic activity</a> by making borrowing more expensive and saving more attractive. </p>

<p>That mechanism works particularly well when consumers are deciding whether to finance a house, purchase a car or take on additional debt. It also discourages businesses from making investments when the expected return is only modestly above their financing costs. As demand slows, businesses have less room to raise prices, easing inflationary pressures.</p>

<p>In this case, the Fed <a href="https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20260916a.htm">justified its move</a> by citing “elevated” inflation and noting that it “will support a timelier return” to its goal of an annual inflation target of 2%. It also suggested the economy would be able to absorb the tightening and described economic activity as “expanding at a solid pace.”</p>

<p>The decision aligns with Fed Chairman <a href="https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/speech/warsh20260828a.htm">Kevin Warsh’s recent comments</a> that restoring price stability is central to the Fed’s credibility. In a key speech in August, he underscored his commitment to bringing annualized inflation back down to 2%, an objective he called a “firm, fixed target” – <a href="https://www.wsj.com/economy/central-banking/the-problem-with-warshs-deference-to-markets-872edf9c">a turnaround</a> from his more ambiguous comments in July. </p>

<p>But in recent months, the economic data has shown that the 2% annual target remains elusive. <a href="https://www.bls.gov/news.release/cpi.nr0.htm">Consumer prices rose</a> 0.4% in August and 3.4% over the past year. Meanwhile, the war with Iran has pushed oil prices back above <a href="https://www.wsj.com/finance/commodities-futures/oil-declines-but-remains-elevated-amid-supply-concerns-geopolitical-risks-15e97c33">US$100 a barrel</a>, adding a new source of inflation pressure through gasoline, diesel, transportation and production costs. </p>

<p>At the same time, the labor market isn’t faltering. The economy added <a href="https://www.bls.gov/news.release/empsit.nr0.htm">162,000 jobs in August</a>, while the unemployment rate remained at 4.1%. The one notable concern is the persistence of long-term joblessness despite the strong headline numbers. More than one-quarter of unemployed Americans have now been out of work for at least six months.</p>

<p>Taken together, those numbers suggested there was room for the Fed to hike rates, given that the economy isn’t sliding into recession. So investors overwhelmingly expected the Fed’s rate increase.</p>

<h2>An uneven economic hit</h2>

<p>However, tighter monetary policy carries a risk: It falls disproportionately on sectors that are already struggling and highly sensitive to interest rates, while having less effect on one of the economy’s strongest sources of demand – the booming AI investment cycle.</p>

<p>Housing provides the clearest example. Persistently high mortgage rates are reinforcing the “<a href="https://www.wsj.com/personal-finance/low-mortgage-rates-home-sales-low-supply-899aab29?mod=article_inline">lock-in</a>” effect for current homeowners. Millions of homeowners financed their houses when mortgage rates were 3% or 4%, so they’re staying put, with little incentive to sell their home and purchase another at much higher rates. </p>

<p>Mortgage rates are mostly influenced by <a href="https://theconversation.com/us-mortgage-rates-are-staying-high-and-the-fed-can-do-very-little-about-it-284417">longer-term factors</a>, including Treasury yields, inflation expectations and market expectations about the future path of interest rates. But the Fed’s decision still matters. Markets increasingly expect today’s hike to be followed by additional increases, signaling that it views inflation as a more persistent risk and putting upward pressure on longer-term interest rates.</p>

<p>That expectation will keep mortgage rates high – probably resulting in fewer home sales, less mobility and continued headwinds for prospective buyers. It’s also likely to make renting relatively more attractive for potential homebuyers who are priced out of buying.</p>

<p>Higher-for-longer rates also change how consumers save. </p>

<p>When interest rates were near zero, they earned almost nothing on safe assets. Today, Treasury securities, money market funds and other relatively safe assets <a href="https://www.nerdwallet.com/investing/news/rate-hike-bond-yields">offer meaningful returns</a>. Higher rates therefore tend to shift incentives throughout the economy away from borrowing and spending and toward saving.</p>

<p>With consumers stretched by inflation and increasingly dipping into their savings, however, this effect may <a href="https://www.economist.com/finance-and-economics/2026/06/21/how-stretched-is-the-american-consumer">be less pronounced</a>. </p>

<h2>The AI sugar high</h2>

<p>When it comes to the AI investment boom, it’s a different picture. Warsh noted in August that <a href="https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/speech/warsh20260828a.htm">more than half of recent capital-spending growth</a> could be attributed to the AI buildout. </p>

<p>The companies that are spending billions of dollars on computing infrastructure are doing so because they <a href="https://www.wsj.com/tech/ai/nvidia-insists-it-can-keep-printing-money-to-fund-the-ai-boom-195e7d5e">expect potentially enormous returns</a> from AI. If those expected returns on investment are exceptionally high, a modest increase in borrowing costs may do little to alter their investment decisions. That stands in sharp contrast to a prospective homebuyer getting sticker shock from <a href="https://www.marketwatch.com/story/30-year-mortgage-rate-jumps-to-7-17-a-nearly-2-year-high-in-the-latest-blow-to-the-housing-market-aadbd63e">mortgage rates nearing 7%</a>.</p>

<p>The federal government, for its part, faces a slower adjustment. A Fed rate hike doesn’t immediately increase the interest rate on all outstanding federal debt. Most Treasury notes and bonds carry fixed rates until they mature. But as the Treasury issues new debt and refinances maturing securities, today’s higher rates gradually become tomorrow’s higher <a href="https://fiscaldata.treasury.gov/interest-expense-avg-interest-rates/">federal interest expense</a>. That rise in interest costs is a main reason some economists <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/14/opinion/national-debt-trump.html">are sounding alarms</a> about the national debt, which recently topped $40 trillion.</p>

<p>In effect, the U.S. economy is facing a reality in which both short- and long-term rates stay higher for longer. The federal government, households and businesses are all adjusting to a borrowing environment that looks substantially different from the one that prevailed for much of the previous decade.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291848/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: If you’re on GLP-1 drugs and plan to fast for Yom Kippur, here’s what you need to know

<title>If you’re on GLP-1 drugs and plan to fast for Yom Kippur, here’s what you need to know</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760302/original/file-20260916-50-camqvj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5760%2C3840&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Fasting for Yom Kippur ends at nightfall with a family meal. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/making-hillel-sandwich-at-passover-seder-royalty-free-image/1384288259">halbergman/E+ via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p><a href="https://lifesciencedaily.news/glp-1-uptake-by-country-where-ozempic-and-mounjaro-are-booming-in-2026/">Millions of people worldwide</a> – as many as <a href="https://www.kff.org/public-opinion/poll-1-in-8-adults-say-they-are-currently-taking-a-glp-1-drug-for-weight-loss-diabetes-or-another-condition-even-as-half-say-the-drugs-are-difficult-to-afford/">1 in 8 adults in the U.S.</a> – are on GLP-1  medication, such as Ozempic, Mounjaro, Wegovy and Zepbound, for treating diabetes or for weight loss. </p>

<p>These drugs are adding a medical twist to religious observances that involve fasting, such as the Jewish holiday of Yom Kippur, which will be observed from sundown on Sept. 20 until nightfall on Sept. 21, 2026. Traditionally, <a href="https://www.chabad.org/library/article_cdo/aid/4489890/jewish/Why-Do-We-Fast-on-Yom-Kippur.htm">fasting on Yom Kippur</a> means forgoing food and water for about 25 hours, which can strongly affect a person’s metabolism. </p>

<p>Other religious traditions include different types of fasts. For example, Muslims who fast during Ramadan neither eat nor drink from dawn to sunset, but they break their fast each night. Christian and Hindu traditions also include dry fasts as well as partial fasts, such as <a href="https://theconversation.com/what-are-the-origins-of-lent-155622">Lent</a> and <a href="https://hindulife.yale.edu/what-navaratri">Navratri</a>, in which people avoid certain foods. </p>

<p>As a <a href="https://hospital.uillinois.edu/find-a-doctor/reed-berger-fleishman">specialist in obesity medicine</a>, I work with many patients who take GLP-1 drugs. Most people can safely fast for Yom Kippur or other religious or cultural observances. But depending on their circumstances, they may need to plan ahead, take certain precautions and be clear on when it’s medically advised that they break their fast. </p>

<h2>Common GLP-1 side effects and fasting</h2>

<p>GLP-1 drugs such as Ozempic, Mounjaro, Wegovy and Zepbound <a href="https://theconversation.com/our-sense-of-taste-helps-pace-our-eating-understanding-how-may-lead-to-new-avenues-for-weight-loss-220373">mimic a natural gut hormone</a>– glucagon-like peptide 1 – that lowers your blood sugar by triggering insulin release when your blood sugar is high. These drugs also slow how quickly food passes through the stomach, which <a href="https://theconversation.com/drugs-that-melt-away-pounds-still-present-more-questions-than-answers-but-ozempic-wegovy-and-mounjaro-could-be-key-tools-in-reducing-the-obesity-epidemic-205549">reduces appetite to aid in weight loss</a>. </p>

<p>GLP-1s have some <a href="https://doi.org/10.1172/JCI194740">common side effects</a> that can occur in anyone taking them, including nausea, vomiting, dizziness, constipation and dehydration. <a href="https://doi.org/10.2147/DMSO.S584175">Fasting may exacerbate them</a>, especially in people who are prone to an upset stomach. GLP-1 side effects are also more common when a patient is increasing their dose, which usually happens monthly as tolerated until they reach their full dosage. </p>

<p>That’s why, if you’re planning to fast for Yom Kippur, it’s best to avoid starting a new GLP-1 medication or increasing the dose of your medication sooner than two weeks or so before the holiday.  </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/DM5cGuddYww?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">GLP-1 drugs work by simulating a gut hormone produced in the body, spurring the release of insulin and slowing down digestion.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>



<h2>Timing your dose</h2>

<p>If you take GLP-1 drugs as weekly injections, which is the most common way of dosing these medications, you should <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.diabres.2017.03.003">stick to your schedule</a> even if you plan to fast. These drugs <a href="https://professional.diabetes.org/standards-of-care">stay in your system </a>during the entire week, so moving or skipping that weekly dose right before fasting can interfere with their effects on blood sugar or weight loss.   </p>

<p>If your weekly injection falls on Yom Kippur, you can generally go ahead and administer it as scheduled. Some patients do report <a href="https://www.drugs.com/medical-answers/how-long-glp-1-nausea-how-you-relief-3582388/">increased nausea on their injection day</a> – if that happens to you, you may wish to delay the injection until after the fast, if you’ve cleared it with your doctor.  </p>

<p>Patients who inject GLP-1 drugs daily may need to adjust the timing. For patients taking these medications for diabetes treatment, it may make sense to do the injection right before the meal that breaks the fast or to hold off until after the fast. This helps reduce the risk of stomach side effects, which can occur when these medications are taken on an empty stomach. </p>

<p>More recently, many patients have switched to <a href="https://www.aamc.org/news/glp-1-pills-weight-loss-are-here-how-will-they-change-obesity-care">oral GLP-1 medications</a>. These pills must generally be taken on an empty stomach with a small amount of water, at a set time before taking any other drugs or any food or beverages. </p>

<p>Because fasting for Yom Kippur includes abstaining from drinking, taking the pill as directed may involve breaking the fast. That means you’ll need to decide in advance whether to take the medicine before the fast begins, after the fast ends or on an alternative schedule. It’s best to avoid simply skipping the daily dose scheduled for Yom Kippur and taking a double dose after the fast.</p>

<p>Skipping the dose won’t be harmful if you’re taking the medication for weight loss. But if you have diabetes, skipping it could dangerously elevate your blood sugar. And doubling the dose later could lead to serious side effects, such as pancreatitis, an inflammation of the pancreas that can lead to hospitalization. </p>

<h2>Diabetes versus weight loss</h2>

<p>If you’re using GLP-1 medications solely for weight management, fasting for 25 hours should not pose serious issues beyond stomach upset. In rare cases, though, combining these drugs with fasting can <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2016.1522">stress the pancreas enough to cause pancreatitis</a>.</p>

<p>Fasting on GLP-1s carries the biggest risks for diabetic patients. That’s because GLP-1 medications are <a href="https://doi.org/10.21037/atm-21-4162">often used alongside other drugs</a> that work primarily by lowering blood sugar, which raises patients’ overall risk of a blood sugar crash.</p>

<p>The greatest concern is in patients taking a GLP-1 medication together with insulin or drugs that stimulate insulin production, such as <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/treatments/sulfonylureas">sulfonylureas</a>. The GLP-1 medication itself may not cause a drop in blood sugar. But because it suppresses appetite and lowers glucose levels, these other medications can magnify the risk of low blood sugar during a prolonged fast.</p>

<p>If that’s your situation, talk to your doctor about whether you can adjust the timing, dose and type of insulin you take and reduce your dose of sulfonylurea in order to fast safely. </p>

<p>In general, people who have Type 1 diabetes or poorly controlled diabetes are <a href="https://doi.org/10.1055/s-0045-1813010">strongly advised not to fast</a> – as are people who: </p>

<ul>
<li>Experience frequent or severe drops in blood sugar.</li>
<li>Have hypoglycemia unawareness – an absence of warning signs for high blood sugar.</li>
<li>Are managing diabetes during pregnancy. </li>
<li>Have severe kidney disease with a high risk of dehydration.</li>
<li>Experience severe gastrointestinal side effects from GLP-1 medications.</li>
</ul>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/UwR36ezpJfc?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Not overeating along with drinking plenty of water beforehand is helpful for anyone fasting – but crucial for people on GLP-1 medications.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>From prefast prep to the post-holiday meal</h2>

<p>Regardless of what GLP-1 medication you take and for what indication, if you plan to fast you’ll need to do some pregaming, monitor how your fast is going and be mindful of how you break it.  </p>

<ul>
<li><p>First, if you are unsure about anything, talk to the clinician who is monitoring your GLP-1 drug treatment so you can decide together whether fasting is safe for you and whether your situation requires any special precautions.</p></li>
<li><p>Before fasting, it’s important to eat a normal meal that includes protein and to avoid both overeating and undereating. Overeating is <a href="https://health.clevelandclinic.org/how-to-manage-glp-1-side-effects">never recommended when on GLP-1 medications</a>, and undereating can set you up for <a href="https://doi.org/10.2147/DMSO.S584175">more side effects during the fast</a>. Although GLP-1 therapy can substantially reduce appetite, patients should avoid skipping the prefast meal entirely.</p></li>
<li><p>GLP-1 medications don’t just decrease appetite – they can also <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s11102-024-01451-7">suppress the body’s natural thirst signals</a>. So before your fast begins, aim to stay hydrated to prevent getting dehydrated while fasting.</p></li>
<li><p>If you are diabetic, make sure you fast under close guidance from your doctor – and make sure you are checking your blood sugar during fasting. Using a glucose monitor is a good idea, particularly if you are taking insulin or other glucose-lowering medications. The goal is for your blood sugar to remain within your usual daily nonfasting range.</p></li>
<li><p>Be ready to break your fast right away if you start feeling dizzy, confused, faint, nauseated or acutely ill, or if your blood sugar dips too low or spikes too high. These symptoms are dangerous and need to be addressed immediately. Stash a rapid source of carbohydrates –  even just some glucose tablets or a few hard candies – within reach so you can access them quickly if needed.</p></li>
<li><p>Finally, plan a gentle, balanced meal to break the fast rather than an unusually large meal, which may provoke nausea, abdominal pain, reflux or vomiting. It’s generally best to avoid higher-fat foods, too, since they can slow down digestion.</p></li>
</ul><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291776/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
