    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760203/original/file-20260916-60-xjz1e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C1023%2C682&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Yemen&#39;s Houthi rebels march in Sanaa, Yemen, on Sept. 10, 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Photos%20show%20Houthi%20rallies%2C%20fighters%20and%20daily%20life%20inside%20Yemen./7b39c4220b0945bfbeb9cbb0e4c99f09/photo">AP Photo</a></span></figcaption></figure><p><em>An advance by Yemen’s Houthi rebels, which has included the targeting of <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/world/middle-east/saudi-arabia-mecca-houthis-drone-iran-war-trump-oil-gas-prices-rcna598075">Saudi cities</a> <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/09/11/world/middleeast/houthis-yemen-red-sea-shipping-maps.html">and infrastructure</a>, has quickly complicated a widening Middle East war.</em></p>

<p><em>Not only has it all but unraveled <a href="https://osesgy.unmissions.org/en/truce-agreement-april-2022">a 2022 truce</a> putting a lid on Yemen’s civil war – in which the Iran-aligned Houthis were fighting a Saudi-led coalition – but the seizure of territory next to the Red Sea has further threatened Saudi energy exports. On Sept. 13, Saudi Arabia and other Arab Gulf nations were due to take part in crucial Omani-hosted talks with Iran in a bid to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. But <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/13/world/middleeast/iran-meeting-gulf-arab-states.html?searchResultPosition=1">they were called off</a>, seemingly over attacks by both the Houthis and Iraqi groups aligned with Tehran.</em></p>

<p><em>The Conversation spoke with <a href="https://www.bakerinstitute.org/expert/kristian-coates-ulrichsen">Gulf analyst</a> Kristian Coates Ulrichsen to help make sense of the dizzying array of intersecting news developments.</em></p>

<h2>What happened with the Oman talks?</h2>

<p>Periodically since the <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/article/iran-war-trump-us-oil-hormuz-key-dates-events.html">war in Iran began on Feb. 28</a>, 2026, and particularly since the <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c4gy700j0eko">signing of the Iran-U.S. memorandum of understanding in mid-June</a>, Omani and Iranian officials have been meeting to discuss how to resolve the blockage in the Strait of Hormuz.</p>

<p>Oman and Iran are the two coastal Gulf States through which the waterway passes, despite Iranian rhetoric about securing and maintaining control over the strait. The challenges facing the negotiators is that Oman will need to build consensus among the other Gulf States for any agreement, as well as the United States, given that one Iranian demand is for passage to be limited to civilian vessels, which would effectively bar U.S. naval ships from the Gulf, including the U.S. Navy’s 5th Fleet, which is headquartered in Bahrain. </p>

<p>Gulf officials – and their U.S. counterparts – would strenuously resist any Iranian attempt to convert their wartime leverage over the strait into a postwar deal that formalizes and regularizes that control.</p>

<p>The <a href="https://apnews.com/article/mideast-news-iran-yemen-houthis-israel-saudi-27d276de911a983cdb1b81101ee56083">postponement of the planned meeting in Oman’s capital Muscat</a> illustrates that the time is not yet right for the talks to proceed and that further dialogue is needed in order to build a consensual framework that can best enable them to succeed. </p>

<h2>How serious are the new attacks on Saudi assets?</h2>

<p>The uptick in <a href="https://www.wsj.com/world/middle-east/yemens-houthi-militants-attack-saudi-energy-infrastructure-067fa4f7">attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure</a> has put in jeopardy the viability of the work-around to Hormuz that enabled the kingdom to maintain oil exports at about half their prewar levels. </p>

<p>Saudi vessels have already started to avoid transiting the <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/why-is-bab-el-mandeb-strait-so-important-2026-09-10/">Bab el-Mandeb</a> Strait and taking the far longer route through the Suez Canal into the Mediterranean and around the coast of Africa. That adds weeks and associated costs to oil exports to predominantly Asian markets. </p>

<p><iframe id="7bAJT" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/7bAJT/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="A map of the Persian Gulf region"></iframe></p>

<p>While the damage to a pumping station that led to the <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/us-energy-chief-says-saudi-arabia-oil-pipeline-should-be-back-within-days-2026-09-15/">temporary closure of the Saudi’s East-West Pipeline</a> was reportedly done by a drone launched from Iraq, the kingdom faces attacks from both its northern and southern neighbors with the range, intent and capability to hit critical energy targets. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A gun-mounted truck leads a convoy of vehicles." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760202/original/file-20260916-50-i8o3e0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760202/original/file-20260916-50-i8o3e0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=382&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760202/original/file-20260916-50-i8o3e0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=382&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760202/original/file-20260916-50-i8o3e0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=382&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760202/original/file-20260916-50-i8o3e0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=480&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760202/original/file-20260916-50-i8o3e0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=480&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760202/original/file-20260916-50-i8o3e0.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=480&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Yemeni security forces escort buses carrying released Houthi detainees as they arrive in Sanaa on Sept. 12, 2026.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/yemeni-security-forces-escort-buses-carrying-released-news-photo/2294895123?adppopup=true">Mohammed Hamoud/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Saudi officials may respond to the latest attacks by rerouting oil back to its east coast facilities on the Persian Gulf, and there has been a steady increase in the volume of oil making its way through Hormuz in recent days and weeks. This return to using the Saudi port at Ras Tanura nevertheless makes oil transportation remain vulnerable to Iranian attacks on shipping in the strait.</p>

<p>Moreover, should the Saudis face a “double choke point” crisis whereby the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait are both effectively shut, there will be no safe and secure way to continue Saudi oil and other industrial exports, or the import of non-oil goods and commodities by ship. </p>

<h2>What options does Saudi Arabia have to respond?</h2>

<p>Saudi Arabia <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2015/mar/26/saudi-arabia-begins-airstrikes-against-houthi-in-yemen">intervened militarily in Yemen</a> in March 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition but quickly got bogged down in an unwinnable conflict. In fact, the major successes in ground operations against the Houthis and other adversaries in Yemen were achieved by the United Arab Emirates rather than Saudi forces. </p>

<p>There is very little appetite in Riyadh for a new military operation in Yemen, especially since the Houthis are skilled in asymmetric combat and have far more advanced drone and other technological capabilities than they possessed during the previous rounds of conflict with Saudi Arabia. </p>

<p>The fact that the Houthis outlasted the two-month U.S. <a href="https://ctc.westpoint.edu/feature-commentary-an-assessment-of-operation-rough-rider/">Operation Rough Rider</a> between March and May 2025 indicates that bombing from the air will not force the Houthis into submission. And the rapid advance made by the Houthis to <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c4g7vr0lngwo">take Mokha and other positions</a> in southwestern Yemen since Sept. 3 suggest that Saudi-trained forces on the ground are insufficient. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A man on a fishing vessels with a commercial tanker seen in the background." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760162/original/file-20260916-50-uo5dd4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C201%2C3857%2C2169&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760162/original/file-20260916-50-uo5dd4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760162/original/file-20260916-50-uo5dd4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760162/original/file-20260916-50-uo5dd4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760162/original/file-20260916-50-uo5dd4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760162/original/file-20260916-50-uo5dd4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760162/original/file-20260916-50-uo5dd4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Fishermen motor past a commercial vessel anchored off Yemen’s coast at Bab al-Mandeb, in the straits connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, on Sept. 12, 2026.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/fishermen-motor-past-a-commercial-vessel-anchored-off-news-photo/2294750914?adppopup=true">AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The Saudi leadership, led by de facto ruler Crown Prince <a href="https://www.cnn.com/world/middleeast/mohammed-bin-salman-fast-facts">Mohammed bin Salman</a>, is instead seeking to put together a multilateral coalition of states that may be able to contribute, in different ways, to ensuring maritime and regional security in and around the Red Sea. This will include the recent signatories Pakistan and Turkey, alongside Saudi Arabia, to the <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/saudi-arabia-turkey-pakistan-sign-joint-defence-deal-amid-regional-turmoil-2026-08-07/">Mecca Joint Defense Agreement</a> and may also include Egypt, which <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/15/egypts-sisi-meets-mbs-backs-saudi-call-for-secure-red-sea-navigation">Crown Prince Mohammed visited on Sept. 15</a>.</p>

<p>Egypt and Turkey may be able to contribute naval assets to assist with maritime patrols in the Red Sea, while Pakistan has long provided Saudi Arabia with soldiers to help protect the kingdom. </p>

<h2>How could this all affect US-Saudi relations?</h2>

<p>Saudi officials, along with counterparts in other Gulf States, <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/iran-warns-gulf-states-tell-trump-desist-or-we-hit-you-hard-2026-08-06/">urged the U.S. and Iran</a> to reach a diplomatic resolution prior to the launch of the war on Feb. 28 and have found themselves caught in the middle of a conflict they sought to avoid. </p>

<p>The perception that the U.S. began the war without a “Plan B” has intersected with the feeling that the U.S. has done little to protect Saudi Arabia and the other Gulf States.</p>

<p>If the White House continues to struggle to make progress in negotiating an end to the war and a resumption of unrestricted passage through the <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/2026/09/16/irans-maximum-leverage-strait-hormuz-has-passed/">Strait of Hormuz</a>, it may be that regional states step in to make a deal of their own. The postponement of the Oman meeting suggests we are not yet at that point. Yet patience may certainly be wearing thin in Riyadh.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292070/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Pardoned by Trump and escaping charges at home, ex-Honduran leader’s case shows a nation’s struggle for sovereignty</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759970/original/file-20260915-50-akwjkd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C1023%2C682&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Former Honduran President Juan Orlando Hernández acknowledges supporters upon his return to Honduras on July 26, 2026.
</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Honduras%20Former%20President%20Case%20Dismissed/0346ff1f3c7141ebbbf84b6525eb270a/photo">AP Photo/Fernando Destephen,File</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>A Honduran judge on Sept. 1, 2026, <a href="https://apnews.com/article/honduras-juan-orlando-hernandez-bf5fb30351d11e7cefabbda8c5b76422">dismissed a sprawling</a> money-laundering and fraud case against the country’s former president, Juan Orlando Hernández. It was the latest stroke of good fortune for Hernández.</p>

<p>Hernández returned home in late July after an eventful four years outside Honduras. He was extradited to the United States in 2022 following a <a href="https://nacla.org/an-absurd-new-chapter-in-the-war-on-drugs/">multiyear, nonpartisan U.S. investigation</a>. In 2024 he was convicted of cocaine trafficking and related charges and <a href="https://www.justice.gov/usao-sdny/pr/juan-orlando-hernandez-former-president-honduras-sentenced-45-years-prison-conspiring">sentenced to 45 years behind bars in the U.S</a>. Yet after serving only 18 months of his sentence, Hernández was <a href="https://apnews.com/article/honduras-us-hernandez-trump-pardon-099332ff4b81bafa3a32c642368ca665">pardoned by President Donald Trump</a>. </p>

<p>Hernández remains a forceful <a href="https://www.laprensa.hn/honduras/tomas-zambrano-reaccion-juan-orlando-hernandez-consejero-partido-nacional-MG31515458#google_vignette">power broker</a> behind the scenes of the current Honduran government, led by President Nasry Asfura of the right-wing National Party. </p>

<p>Yet as a <a href="https://www.unr.edu/political-science/people/laura-blume">scholar of Latin American politics</a>, I believe Hernández’s return to Honduras, and his successes evading legal accountability, are emblematic of something broader than impunity for elites: His case demonstrates the struggle for sovereignty in a country facing a renewed form of U.S. intervention.</p>

<h2>Politics under the shadow of US intervention</h2>

<p>Hernández’s return to Honduras on July 26 was symbolic. He landed at Palmerola International Airport, which shares its runway with the Soto Cano Air Base, a <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-us-policy-in-honduras-set-the-stage-for-todays-migration-65935">longtime staging ground of U.S. interventions</a> in Honduras. </p>

<p>While Hernández was greeted by <a href="https://contracorriente.red/2026/07/26/el-regreso-del-joh-a-honduras-despues-del-indulto-de-trump/">National Party supporters</a>, for many Hondurans his pardon and return to the country were seen to undermine <a href="https://criterio.hn/adios-joh-el-grito-de-honduras-para-celebrar-la-extradicion-de-juan-orlando-hernandez/">hopes for justice</a> and adversely affect the political process.</p>

<p>When Trump first <a href="https://www.npr.org/2025/11/28/nx-s1-5624478/trump-plans-to-pardon-juan-orlando-hernandez">announced plans to pardon Hernández</a>, it was on the eve of the Honduran elections in November 2025. In another sign of meddling from Washington, Trump <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/trump-says-he-hopes-honduras-elects-conservative-national-partys-asfura-2025-11-26/">endorsed</a> Asfura and <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2025/12/2/honduras-election-why-has-trump-threatened-to-cut-off-aid">threatened to cut off aid</a> to Honduras if Asfura, who was trailing in <a href="https://www.as-coa.org/articles/poll-tracker-honduras-2025-presidential-election">opinion polls leading up to the elections</a>, did not win. </p>

<p>On Dec. 1, the day after the election and with Asfura and center-right politician Salvador Nasralla locked in a technical tie as vote counting continued, Trump issued a full pardon for Hernández. U.S. officials then hurried to provide <a href="https://www.propublica.org/article/trump-ice-pardon-juan-orlando-hernandez-honduras-prison-special-treatment">special immigration protections</a> for Hernández, and a <a href="https://www.propublica.org/article/trump-ice-pardon-juan-orlando-hernandez-honduras-prison-special-treatment">specialized tactical team</a> drove him from a West Virginia prison to the luxury Waldorf Astoria hotel in Manhattan. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">

            </figcaption>

<p>Back in Honduras, the pardon was seen as a “<a href="https://www.propublica.org/article/trump-ice-pardon-juan-orlando-hernandez-honduras-prison-special-treatment">green light for the National Party to manipulate the vote</a>,” as a former high-ranking U.S. diplomat told ProPublica. Trump’s actions signaled that Washington supported the National Party’s engagement in electoral manipulation, as election observers and <a href="https://muse.jhu.edu/article/852749">academic experts say</a> <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2017/12/18/hernandez-declared-winner-in-honduras-disputed-election">happened in 2017</a> with Hernández’s unconstitutional second presidential term election. </p>

<p>Following weeks of <a href="https://www.wlrn.org/light/americas/2025-12-16/honduras-election-president-trump-vote-count">suspicious delays</a> and <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2025/12/25/world/americas/honduras-election-dispute.html">fraud allegations</a>, Asfura was <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2025/12/24/americas/honduras-presidential-election-results-latam-intl">announced the winner on Dec. 24, 2025</a>, by a margin of less than 1 percent. </p>

<h2>A legacy of impunity in Honduras</h2>

<p>Although free from the U.S. justice system, Hernández still potentially faced charges in Honduras. </p>

<p>On Dec. 9 the Honduran attorney general <a href="https://apnews.com/article/honduras-hernandez-pardon-president-trump-arrest-order-049a016373f30736e4825ac4a682e7e8">reactivated an international arrest warrant for Hernández</a> over charges of fraud and money laundering. </p>

<p>These charges are part of the corruption case known as <a href="https://pulitzercenter.org/stories/exclusive-pandoras-box-corruption-honduras">Pandora</a>, a scheme that embezzled $12 million in public funding and allegedly <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/honduras-prosecutors-accuse-two-ex-presidents-diverting-public-funds-campaigns-2023-10-11/">diverted that money into political campaigns</a>, including Hernández’s 2013 presidential campaign.</p>

<p>Previous Pandora trials accused <a href="https://www.univision.com/univision-news/latin-america/whos-who-in-honduras-pandoras-box-of-corruption">major National Party figures</a>, yet during Hernández’s presidency a special appeals court <a href="https://insightcrime.org/news/honduras-buries-pandora-case-remnants-anti-corruption-fight/">dismissed the cases</a>. But under the left-leaning administration of Xiomara Castro – from 2022 to 2026 – Honduras <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/honduras-prosecutors-accuse-two-ex-presidents-diverting-public-funds-campaigns-2023-10-11/">in 2023 indicted</a> former National Party presidents Hernández and his predecessor, Porfirio Lobo. </p>

<p>Hernández remained in the U.S. until his international arrest warrant was suspended, returning to Honduras shortly before his <a href="https://www.wlrn.org/americas/2026-08-04/a-honduran-judge-grants-former-president-juan-orlando-hernandez-release-as-corruption-trial-proceeds">initial trial</a>. On Aug. 12, 2026, the Public Ministry confirmed the charges against Hernández and <a href="https://criterio.hn/juez-aplaza-audiencia-inicial-contra-joh-tras-peticion-de-la-defensa/">presented 48 pieces of evidence</a>. Yet after two weeks, the <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/2/honduran-court-drops-case-against-ex-president-hernandez-after-trump-pardon">court dropped the charges against Hernández</a>.</p>

<p>With the <a href="https://inkstickmedia.com/trumps-pardon-power-undermines-the-law-at-home-and-abroad/">National Party back in power</a>, few believed Hernández could be held accountable in Honduras, particularly given that the Honduran judicial system is plagued by <a href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10714839.2024.2388373">targeted violence</a> that undermines the rule of law.</p>

<p>Indeed, <a href="https://global.oup.com/academic/product/the-art-of-trafficking-9780197818190">impunity is virtually guaranteed</a> for the wealthy and powerful. And that is something Hernández helped ensure. </p>

<p>Under his presidency, Honduras passed legal reforms specifically <a href="https://insightcrime.org/news/honduras-buries-pandora-case-remnants-anti-corruption-fight/">reducing sentences for money laundering</a> and <a href="https://insightcrime.org/news/why-money-launderers-honduras-may-be-getting-away-with-it/">protecting politicians from investigations for embezzlement</a>. Foreshadowing the likely outcome of Hernández’s trial, Lobo was <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x5BSk8sqOUc">acquitted</a> days before Hernández’s return.</p>

<h2>The right-wing push for the region</h2>

<p>Although Hernández’s trial is over, controversy over his return remains. That’s in part because of explosive new allegations that surfaced in May 2026. </p>

<p>The Spanish media outlet Canal Red released <a href="https://therealnews.com/hondurasgate-leaks-far-right-plan-to-undermine-latin-americas-left">37 audio messages</a> allegedly with the voices of politicians, including Asfura and Hernández. According to the leaked audio files, a scandal known as <a href="https://www.dropsitenews.com/p/hondurasgate-leaked-audio-files-juan-orlando-hernandez-likely-authentic">HondurasGate</a>, Hernández’s return was merely one part of an international scheme to undermine left-wing Latin American governments and expand foreign militarization in Honduras. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Demonstrators rally in a public square." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760214/original/file-20260916-50-mzn1bw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760214/original/file-20260916-50-mzn1bw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760214/original/file-20260916-50-mzn1bw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760214/original/file-20260916-50-mzn1bw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760214/original/file-20260916-50-mzn1bw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760214/original/file-20260916-50-mzn1bw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760214/original/file-20260916-50-mzn1bw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">

<p>Those implicated dismiss the files as AI-generated propaganda. While <a href="https://reactionary.international/investigations/hondurasgate/en/">independent analysis</a> suggests the files are <a href="https://www.dropsitenews.com/p/hondurasgate-leaked-audio-files-juan-orlando-hernandez-likely-authentic">likely authentic</a>, <a href="https://www.expedientepublico.org/la-telarana-detras-de-red-en-el-hondurasgate/">valid suspicions from independent sources</a> have <a href="https://www.expedientepublico.org/especial/hondurasgate-escandalo-o-desinformacion-con-marca-rusa/">emerged casting doubt</a> on their veracity. </p>

<p>Regardless of the HondurasGate audios’ authenticity, much of what they outline echoes wider concerns over external pressures reshaping the region’s politics and expanding militarization.</p>

<p>Trump has been open about seeking to secure <a href="https://foreignpolicy.com/2026/03/10/shield-americas-trump-us-right-wing-leaders-cartels-security-military/">right-wing allies throughout the Americas</a>. Weeks after pardoning Hernández’s narco-trafficking, the Trump administration raided Venezuela to arrest President Nicolás Maduro on alleged narco-trafficking charges.</p>

<p>Meanwhile, the U.S. continues to use sanctions in Cuba in an aggressive push for <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/20/us-pummels-cuban-economy-with-new-sanctions-on-mining-construction">regime change on the island</a>, and has used varying degrees of influence to try to affect elections in <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/jun/30/the-guardian-view-on-colombias-election-trumpism-has-gone-transnational">places from Colombia</a> <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/07/31/nx-s1-5913705/brazils-president-accuses-u-s-of-attempting-to-interfere-with-countrys-election">to Brazil</a>.</p>

<p>In Honduras, the National Party – and especially Hernández – has been a willing partner in tying its own national priorities to those of the U.S. and close U.S. allies, including Israel. </p>

<p>Hernández cultivated strategic importance as an ally of <a href="https://www.gov.il/en/pages/spoke_honduras210920">Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu</a> and Trump. <a href="https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/politics-and-diplomacy/israel-to-modernize-honduran-fighter-jets-and-helicopters-475042">Israel</a> and the <a href="https://nacla.org/honduras-narco-state-made-in-the-united-states/">U.S.</a> have long provided military technology and security aid to Honduras, and both are expanding military involvement there.</p>

<p>Recently, Honduras signed a memorandum <a href="https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/defense-news/article-905721">expanding defense cooperation with Israel</a>, and <a href="https://www.war.gov/News/Speeches/Speech/Article/4572686/secretary-of-war-pete-hegseth-delivers-remarks-at-the-americas-counter-cartel-c/">U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth</a> announced agreements for joint military operations on Honduran, Colombian and Guatemalan soil, similar to ones in <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/03/us/politics/us-ecuador-trump-military-operations.html">Ecuador</a>. </p>

<h2>An outside corporate frenzy</h2>

<p>The <a href="https://history.cornell.edu/news/silicon-valley-driving-trumps-policy-honduras">motivation behind Trump’s support</a> for Asfura’s election and Hernández’s return is also related to advancing controversial charter zones in Honduras known as ZEDEs, the Spanish acronym for Zones for Employment and Economic Development.</p>

<p>Trump allies in Silicon Valley, including <a href="https://truthout.org/articles/peter-thiel-is-unleashing-a-neocolonial-billionaire-fantasy-in-honduras/">Peter Thiel</a> of PayPal and <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-interactive/2025/sep/22/ice-palantir-data">Palantir</a>, are leading investors in <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2024/08/28/magazine/prospera-honduras-crypto.html">Próspera</a>, one of the ZEDEs. </p>

<p><a href="https://www.nlginternational.org/report/Final_NLG_ZEDE_Report.pdf">Passed in 2013</a> under Hernández, the ZEDEs are a highly contested sociopolitical experiement; they create spaces of privatized governance within Honduras that essentially forfeit Honduran <a href="https://contracorriente.red/2025/03/31/soberania-e-inmortalidad-el-tesoro-perdido-que-los-tecnofeudales-buscan-en-honduras/">sovereignty</a> to U.S. <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/08/10/nx-s1-5925350/the-nerd-reich-tracks-the-unmasking-of-silicon-valleys-true-politics">tech titans</a> seeking havens from government regulations and oversight. </p>

<p>The ZEDEs were deemed unconstitutional under the Castro administration, leading Próspera’s <a href="https://jacobin.com/2023/11/honduras-international-law-isds-thiel-prospera-free-market-neocolonialism">billionaire investors to sue Honduras</a> for nearly $11 billion. Now, with the National Party back in power, a renewed <a href="https://ips-dc.org/report-corporate-assault-on-honduras/">corporate push</a> is underway and the ZEDEs are moving forward rapidly, including in <a href="https://contracorriente.red/2026/07/10/empresa-extranjera-promueve-proyecto-de-ciudad-autonoma-en-la-moskitia-hondurena-comunidad-denuncia-falta-de-consulta/">Afro-Indigenous territories</a>.</p>

<h2>A warning for the region</h2>

<p>Ultimately, Hernández’s case shows the extent to which a right-wing vision is currently winning in Honduras and, from critics’ standpoint, the risks that vision poses to democratic governance and sovereignty. </p>

<p>As foreign corporations and billionaires secure access to Honduran resources, average Hondurans are struggling. There have been <a href="https://www.resumenlatinoamericano.org/2026/08/04/honduras-masacre-laboral-de-empleados-publicos-continua-y-preguntan-donde-estan-sus-prestaciones/">massive politicized</a> <a href="http://hondudiario.com/2026/07/13/secretaria-de-trabajo-advierte-que-7-de-cada-10-empleados-despedidos-demandan-al-estado/">layoffs in the public sector</a>. Doctors in the public health system report going months without pay since President Asfura, who also named himself <a href="https://www.infobae.com/honduras/2026/01/28/nasry-asfura-anuncia-primer-bloque-de-su-gabinete-y-asume-directamente-la-secretaria-de-salud/">secretary of health</a>, entered office. Meanwhile, private healthcare and agribusiness have received <a href="https://english.elpais.com/international/2026-08-01/honduras-under-nasry-asfura-state-cuts-violence-and-the-shadow-of-juan-orlando-hernandez.html">multimillion-dollar government contracts</a>.</p>

<p>At the same time, ongoing U.S. immigration crackdowns are <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y7uKIpJE51I">hurting the Honduran economy</a>, which is heavily dependent on remittances. While Hernández remained in the U.S. until he was safe to return to Honduras, the same is not true for <a href="https://hondurasdaily.com/story/2026-06-17-honduran-deportations-surge-43-through-may-2026">thousands of Hondurans</a> who are being deported, often <a href="https://nacla.org/u-s-government-eliminates-legal-protections-for-honduran-women/">despite fears of violence</a>.</p>

<p>Yet while ordinary Hondurans face rising insecurity, including increasing <a href="https://www.infobae.com/honduras/2026/08/12/honduras-registra-1236-homicidios-en-el-primer-semestre-de-2026/">homicides</a> and <a href="https://contracorriente.red/2026/04/08/aumentan-homicidios-y-desapariciones-en-honduras-policias-cuestionados/">disappearances</a>, a <a href="https://www.laprensa.hn/honduras/juan-orlando-hernandez-regresa-honduras-proteccion-especial-estado-EI31286651">special unit of Honduran forces</a> was designated to protect Hernández. </p>

<p>That’s the privileged political environment Hernández spent his career building – and from which he again directly benefits back in Honduras.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290009/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Even the Buddha experienced challenges with meditation: Historical texts reveal its potential downsides</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759109/original/file-20260910-50-p03snj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C8192%2C5461&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Meditation may not always be beneficial, researchers say.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/adult-arab-male-with-a-ponytail-meditating-in-a-royalty-free-image/1483989816?phrase=meditation&amp;searchscope=image,film&amp;adppopup=true">AzmanJaka/E+ via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>As a scholar of “<a href="https://www.buddhistmedicine.net/">Buddhist medicine</a>,” I have studied the connections between Buddhism and well-being since the late 1990s. During the course of that research, I would periodically run into sources claiming that meditation could sometimes have unexpected or adverse health effects. When I discovered in 2020 that <a href="https://www.cheetahhouse.org/vce">psychologists were beginning to document</a> the same thing, I began to examine more systematically how Buddhist texts address this issue. </p>

<p>I started coordinating a team of colleagues who translate Pali, Sanskrit, Chinese, Tibetan, Japanese and other languages to gather sources from around the Buddhist world, which we published in a 2026 book, “<a href="https://uhpress.hawaii.edu/title/meditation-sickness-a-sourcebook-on-the-dangers-of-buddhist-practice/">Meditation Sickness: A Sourcebook on the Dangers of Buddhist Practice</a>.” We included scriptures and historical documents but also autobiographies of sufferers and advice from contemporary teachers from across Asia. </p>

<p>What emerges from these collections is the certainty that Buddhism had never understood meditation to be without its dangers. However, the sources also contain potentially valuable advice for what to do when meditation goes wrong. </p>

<h2>Scientists are reevaluating meditation</h2>

<p>Decades of scientific research have established the health benefits of mindfulness and other meditation practices, making them a ubiquitous part of today’s global wellness industry. But some researchers have been questioning whether meditation is necessarily safe for everyone. Starting in 2017, psychologist <a href="https://vivo.brown.edu/display/wbritton">Willoughby Britton</a>, religion scholar <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=f06ZnhcAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">Jared Lindahl</a> and their team of researchers at Brown University have documented cases of meditation leading to harm rather than wellness. </p>

<p>Their study, titled <a href="https://www.cheetahhouse.org/vce">The Varieties of Contemplative Experience</a>, involved in-depth interviews with nearly 100 Western Buddhist practitioners and teachers who experienced difficulties – including fear, anxiety, panic, paranoia and other negative experiences – while engaging in different meditation practice traditions. </p>

<p><a href="https://www.cheetahhouse.org/bibliography">Other studies</a> have reported similar findings, suggesting that between 3% and 65% of practitioners may experience adverse effects from mindfulness or other forms of contemplative practice. </p>

<h2>Buddhist texts have long described meditation challenges</h2>

<p>Meanwhile, Asian Buddhist traditions have been talking about the potential dangers of meditation for millennia. One common name for meditation-related challenges in East Asia has been “<a href="https://blogs.dickinson.edu/buddhistethics/files/2023/08/Salguero-Finalized-ms-for-publication47.pdf">meditation sickness</a>”  – “chanbing” in Chinese, or “zenbyō” in Japanese. They are also commonly diagnosed as disorders of “wind” – “loong” in Tibetan, “lom” in Thai.</p>

<p>Some historical texts describe the Buddha’s own challenges with meditation. In a Pali text commonly dated to the early centuries C.E. called the <a href="https://wisdomexperience.org/ebook/the-middle-length-discourses-of-the-buddha/part-one-the-root-fifty-discourses-mulapa%E1%B9%87%E1%B9%87asapa%E1%B8%B7i/4-the-great-division-of-pairs-mahayamakavagga/36-mahasaccaka-sutta-the-greater-discourse-to-saccaka/">Great Discourse to Saccaka</a>, for example, the Buddha recounts experiencing headaches and other symptoms as a result of overconcentration.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759111/original/file-20260910-60-g2o41z.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A granite statue of a seated Buddha in meditation." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759111/original/file-20260910-60-g2o41z.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759111/original/file-20260910-60-g2o41z.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759111/original/file-20260910-60-g2o41z.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759111/original/file-20260910-60-g2o41z.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759111/original/file-20260910-60-g2o41z.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759111/original/file-20260910-60-g2o41z.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759111/original/file-20260910-60-g2o41z.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Many other sources describe similar experiences happening to other people. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1515/9780824886868-010">Secret Essentials for Curing Meditation Sickness</a>, a fifth-century scripture from the Silk Roads kingdom of Khotan, narrates how adept meditators “went mad” when loud sounds startled them while deep in meditation.</p>

<p>Two major scriptures – the Sanskrit <a href="https://huntingtonarchive.org/resources/downloads/sutras/02Prajnaparamita/Astasahasrika.pdf">Perfection of Insight in 8,000 Lines</a> from the first to second century C.E., and the Chinese <a href="https://blogs.dickinson.edu/buddhistethics/files/2023/08/Salguero-Finalized-ms-for-publication47.pdf">Shurangama Sutra</a>, from the eighth century C.E – relate how advanced spiritual practitioners can be vulnerable to attack by “demons.” Whether such demons are understood as external entities or as psychological manifestations is a matter of interpretation in Buddhist traditions.</p>

<p>One story from the <a href="https://jocbs.org/index.php/jocbs/article/view/99/119">Samyukta Agama</a>, dating to the early centuries C.E. and available in multiple languages, even tells of monks who committed suicide en masse after practicing a meditation the Buddha had taught, prompting him to modify his instructions.</p>

<h2>What to do when things go wrong</h2>

<p>One clear takeaway from these Asian Buddhist perspectives on meditation is that side effects are no one’s fault; they are the acknowledged risks of a powerful set of transformative practices. But they are also manageable. While Buddhist sources point out the potential dangers of meditation, many also describe what to do when things go wrong. </p>

<p>Meditation masters and physicians from across Asia have devoted substantial attention to <a href="https://uhpress.hawaii.edu/title/meditation-sickness-a-sourcebook-on-the-dangers-of-buddhist-practice/">diagnosing and treating practice-related illness</a> with different types of counterbalancing meditations, visualization, chanting, acupuncture, herbs and other remedies. One common type of treatment involves “grounding,” or redirecting attention to the lower abdomen, the feet, or a point deep in the ground below the body. </p>

<p>Another type of grounding involves visualizing energy descending through the body from head to toe. A 17th-century Japanese monk named Hakuin Ekaku, for example, <a href="https://tricycle.org/magazine/meditation-sickness/">describes visualizing butter melting</a> on the crown of the head and slowly oozing downward, relaxing everything it touches until it reaches the ground.  </p>

<p>Whether this accumulated wisdom about how to deal with the side effects of Buddhist practice can be translated into forms useful for contemporary practitioners remains an open question for scholarly study. Addressing this question is a priority of the <a href="https://meditationsickness.com/collaborations/">Contemplative Challenges Collective</a>, a research initiative that I launched earlier this year.</p>

<h2>Informed consent for meditation?</h2>

<p>Asian Buddhist traditions also stress that it is crucial to distinguish between the normal healthy challenges of doing something transformative on the one hand and a true medical crisis on the other. In fact, <a href="https://theconversation.com/mindfulness-is-often-presented-as-a-path-to-calm-but-its-buddhist-roots-explain-why-it-can-also-bring-difficulties-285314">Buddhist texts say</a> that people can expect challenges to arise as part of the process of spiritual development. </p>

<p>Navigating difficult psychological territory – especially encountering one’s traumas and core fears – can be quite difficult and also tremendously rewarding at the same time. </p>

<p>My research shows that Buddhist cultures differ on what crosses a line from expected challenges to debilitating mental and physical conditions. What constitutes a health crisis in ancient India or medieval China is different from 18th-century Japan or 21st-century Tibet. What is tolerable in a community of monastics dedicated to deep contemplative practice will be different from what is reasonable for everyday people interested in stress reduction. </p>

<p>How to navigate the benefits and dangers of mindfulness and other meditations is something that every culture and community must work out for itself. It’s yet another aspect of how Buddhism needs to be continually translated into our own time and place and adapted to harmonize with our own needs and cultural expectations. </p>

<p>In the West, many meditation teachers and researchers alike are now calling for <a href="https://www.cheetahhouse.org/about-us/#mission">informed consent</a>, better screening and training for teachers and clinicians to recognize when practice has the potential to become dangerous. Some experts feel that therapeutic meditation <a href="https://greatergood.berkeley.edu/article/item/why_meditation_might_need_a_warning_label">should carry a warning label</a>, like any other medical intervention that is both a potential cure and a potential risk. </p>

<p>Western promoters, practitioners, app developers and scholars of meditation alike have long ignored, dismissed or been completely unaware of the potential downsides. But the inconvenient fact that meditation is not always beneficial has long been familiar to the Buddhist tradition, which has a lot to say on this topic that may prove helpful.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/287741/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Why an overactive immune system attacks the bodies of people with lupus but still leaves them vulnerable to infection</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759680/original/file-20260914-50-y3m217.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C1948%2C1298&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Lupus can cause a painful, widespread rash.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/mature-woman-scratching-her-neck-royalty-free-image/2275283938">pocketlight/E+ via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Despite having an overactive immune system, people with lupus may still struggle to fight bacterial infections. My team and I found that this paradox may be <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cpblue.2026.100080">because chronic inflammation</a> pushes their immune cells toward the wrong kind of response.</p>

<p>To understand why an overactive immune system can still fail to control bacterial infection, we focused on <a href="https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/body/22313-neutrophils">neutrophils</a>, which are white blood cells that are among the first to respond when bacteria enter the body. Neutrophils can release webs of DNA and antimicrobial proteins called <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/nri.2017.105">neutrophil extracellular traps, or NETs</a>, that can trap bacteria, limiting their spread and killing them.</p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759686/original/file-20260914-50-p7bxqh.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Three microscopy images of what looks like a perforated net, zooming in to reveal a mass of fibers" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759686/original/file-20260914-50-p7bxqh.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759686/original/file-20260914-50-p7bxqh.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=1823&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759686/original/file-20260914-50-p7bxqh.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=1823&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759686/original/file-20260914-50-p7bxqh.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=1823&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759686/original/file-20260914-50-p7bxqh.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=2291&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759686/original/file-20260914-50-p7bxqh.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=2291&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759686/original/file-20260914-50-p7bxqh.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=2291&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Neutrophil extracellular traps (arrow in image C) trap pathogens in the body for destruction. Image A shows a bronchiole in the lungs infected with the fungus <em>Candida albicans</em>, and image B zooms in on the boxed area.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="http://doi.org/10.1371/journal.ppat.1000639">Urban et al/PLoS Pathogens</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/">CC BY-SA</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Scientists often discuss these traps as if they are all the same, but the body can <a href="https://doi.org/10.1101/cshperspect.a037028">produce NETs through different pathways</a>, and they do not all work equally well.</p>

<p>For example, healthy neutrophils responding to infection from <em>Staphylococcus aureus</em> can sense lactate, a chemical byproduct made by the bacteria. That signal helps <a href="https://theconversation.com/mitochondria-can-sense-bacteria-and-trigger-your-immune-system-to-trap-them-revealing-new-ways-to-treat-infections-and-autoimmunity-255939">trigger neutrophils to release a type of NET</a> that serves as a trap rich in antibacterial proteins, but also kills the neutrophil.</p>

<p>In lupus, my team and I found that inflammatory molecules <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cpblue.2026.100080">interfere with this antibacterial response</a> in mice. These signals reduced levels of a protein needed to sense bacterial lactate. At the same time, another inflammatory molecule pushed neutrophils toward another form of NET it could release more quickly, sparing the neutrophil but less effective at killing bacteria.</p>

<p>The result is not an immune system that is weak, but an immune response that is highly active but misdirected.</p>

<h2>Why it matters</h2>

<p>Lupus is <a href="https://www.niams.nih.gov/health-topics/lupus">usually described as an autoimmune disease</a> in which the immune system attacks the body’s own tissues. But <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/rheumatology/keaa478">serious infections are also a major concern</a> for people with lupus. Some of that risk comes from medications that suppress the immune system, but the disease itself can also alter how immune cells function. </p>

<p>Our findings help explain why more inflammation does not necessarily mean better protection from infection. The type and timing of the immune response matter.</p>

<p>We also found that treatments currently used for lupus can correct specific defects in these neutrophil pathways. Our results do not show that people taking standard lupus treatments will have fewer infections, but they do suggest that existing therapies can correct immune defects that may contribute to susceptibility to infection.</p>

<h2>What still isn’t known</h2>

<p>The immune system is more complicated than one cell type or one response. Although we found that standard lupus treatments reduced the number of bacteria in several organs in lupus-prone mice, they did not significantly improve survival compared with untreated mice. Other immune cells, tissue damage and additional features of lupus likely contribute to poor outcomes during infection.</p>

<p>There is also an ongoing debate about what neutrophil extracellular traps actually do in lupus. Some studies have found that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1172/jci.insight.92926">disrupting pathways required for NETs to form</a> does not necessarily improve lupus, challenging the idea that simply making more NETs drives the disease. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/hqRjibvSpRM?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Lupus can cause physically and emotionally painful symptoms.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Our findings suggest that what kind of NET neutrophils make and under what circumstances may be more important questions for lupus. During infection, lupus neutrophils may produce a type of NET that is less effective at killing bacteria while still releasing inflammatory material. That combination of poor infection control together with an inappropriate inflammatory response might exacerbate lupus.</p>

<h2>What’s next</h2>

<p>My team and I are now focused on understanding how different types of NETs affect autoimmune disease and infection. Rather than treating all NETs as the same response, we want to define how different NETs are generated, what they contain and whether particular kinds are protective or harmful in different contexts. </p>

<p>Understanding how lupus changes the type of NET response produced during infection may help explain why disease activity, infection risk and treatment response vary among patients.</p>

title: Trump’s failed Fed takeover
excerpt: Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh at a news conference on September 16, 2026. | Andrew Harnik/Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily new
body: Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh at a news conference on September 16, 2026. | Andrew Harnik/Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here

Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump’s Fed gambit has officially failed.  What happened? On Wednesday, the Federal Reserve voted to raise interest rates by a quarter of a percent, citing ongoing inflation

The rate hike was widely expected, and normally it would be largely unremarkable (at least for this newsletter, which doesn’t generally cover monetary policy).  In this case, however, it’s also a direct rebuke to Trump, who has spent the last year-and-a-half-plus demanding rate cuts — and plotting a Fed takeover to get them.  How has Trump gone after the Fed? It’s a long list, but the two most significant episodes are Trump’s efforts to force Fed governor Lisa Cook from her seat to stack the Fed board in his favor ( still ongoing ) and the Justice Department’s coercive criminal investigation against former Fed chair Jerome Powell ( since ended ).  Neither succeeded, but Trump likely thought his goal was in reach when the Senate confirmed his nominee for Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, in May
On Wednesday, however, Warsh — several months into a four-year term as Fed chair — bucked Trump’s persistent demands by voting for the rate hike
Why does this matter? Trump successfully exerting political control over the Fed would be extremely bad news for just about everyone
Lowering interest rates is a great way to juice the economy in the short term — exactly what he might want as his party faces down a potential midterm wipeout

But it could seriously damage the economy’s long-term health too, which is why the Fed is designed — successfully, as it turns out — to be insulated from partisan politics.  What else should I know? So far, Trump’s response to the hike has been muted, at least by his standards.  He’s threatened to take more drastic action, however: Earlier this month, he said he would suspend trade relations “WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT” if the Fed went through with its rate hike
It’s not clear whether he’ll make good on that threat — but one way or another, we likely haven’t heard the last of Trump’s Fed vendetta

And with that, it’s time to log off… Here’s a small bit of good news from New York: After an announcement by Mayor Zohran Mamdani earlier this year, the city is rolling out new, free public restrooms this week as part of a pilot program to address a longstanding complaint by New Yorkers.  Have a great evening and we’ll see you back here tomorrow!

title: Should we be skeptical about the AI panic?
excerpt: AI risk activists protest near Downing Street in London, England, on on September 16, 2026. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images Is AI going to kill us all?  In Sili
body: AI risk activists protest near Downing Street in London, England, on on September 16, 2026. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images Is AI going to kill us all?  In Silicon Valley, it’s not such a novel question

But after Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon quit his job last week and posted on X that AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade,” a lot more people are asking. “This is not a marketing stunt,” Coxon wrote . “If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible – but I hear the same people express fear privately
No other human activity poses this level of danger.” Coxon is far from alone in his assessment — some current Anthropic employees agree — but his post struck a particular chord
The AI industry quickly weighed in, with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei calling for an industry-wide slowdown on frontier AI research
Other AI leaders, including Sam Altman and Elon Musk, have done the same
To break down whether we really need to worry about a robot apocalypse, Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram spoke to Wired senior writer Maxwell Zeff

According to Zeff, “there are a lot of people in Silicon Valley right now who are warning that that’s a real possibility.” But not everyone agrees, and they certainly don’t agree on what to do about it
Below is an excerpt of Sean’s conversation with Zeff, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify

Are we all going to die at the hands of AI? There are a lot of people in Silicon Valley right now who are warning that that’s a real possibility.  The thing that people have to understand is that Silicon Valley has been calling for added attention on AI safety for years
So when this Anthropic researcher said last week that he was worried that AI could kill humanity in the next few years, that was shocking to many people
My parents, my family called me, and they were worried, understandably
They asked me the same question: “Are we going to die?” And I had to tell them, these people have been worried about AI killing all of us for years, and now it seems to be breaking through
What was it about this statement from Jacob Coxon that broke through? I interviewed Jacob, and the thing he said to me is that he thinks this is just the right time
Anthropic is about to go public in what could be the biggest IPO ever
The Trump administration is focused on AI in a way that no other presidency has ever been before

And of course, yes, the Hugging Face incident everyone just heard about, you talked about it on your show a few weeks ago .  People are starting to become aware that these AI systems are getting really good, and the companies that are building them don’t seem to understand how to control them
His tweet got more than 150 million views on X

And it also was a big wake-up call to lawmakers and leaders in Silicon Valley and saying, “This is a moment for action.” Are there people who are pushing back? One of the most interesting pushbacks that this got was from David Sacks, who is an adviser to the Trump administration on AI

He has called out a lot of this as “doomerism” and said that these calls for AI to slow down are the AI industry warning about the technology that they’re building and advocating for regulatory capture
There’s a lot of skeptics in Silicon Valley who think that this is just another person in the AI safety community that is blowing the whistle
The view of a lot of venture capitalists and investors and startup founders in Silicon Valley is that we don’t need some big regulation to protect us from AI risks
We just need to uplift more players in the space
In fact, it’s the doomers and the fatalists who do, right? Because Jacob’s call only leads to more calls right up to the top of Anthropic

What this all leads to is [Anthropic CEO] Dario Amodei [posting] a blog saying that we need to “pace the frontier.” This is a call for the entire AI industry, not just Anthropic, not just OpenAI, but also Google, Meta, Microsoft, Amazon, all the big tech companies in America, to get together and slow down their AI development
This doesn’t mean they’re going to stop building AI altogether
They’re still going to put their products out into the world
They’re still going to try to improve them, but they just want to make it a little slower than it would be if it was completely uncontained
Amodei really asks for three specific things:  The first thing is, AI companies should have these independent evaluators inside of them
This is a common thing in other industries like the banking industry or the airline industry

People come in to make sure that these companies are doing safe things.  The second thing is this collaborative effort from American AI companies [on safety], and that actually will need to involve the US government to allow this to happen

The US government, he says, may need to issue some sort of waiver, some sort of law that says they can go ahead and coordinate on safety.  The third thing is this international slowdown, this international agreement between China and the US and Europe to say, “Hey, we recognize that this is akin to a nuclear arms race and it’s too dangerous for all of us to be competing with each other.” All these guys are responsible for the rapid acceleration of AI models in our lives, collaborations with the Defense Department, God knows what else
And they’re all coming out over the weekend at the exact same time after this whistleblower and saying, “Yeah, dude, slow this thing down
This thing’s crazy.” Should we be skeptical? It is very fair to be skeptical of this claim
One thing that these AI companies have realized in the last year is that AI is extremely unpopular
Recent polling suggests that a majority of Americans think AI is developing too fast
They think it’s going to take their jobs
Maybe you’ve heard — data centers are not very popular.  By calling to pace the frontier and saying, “We’re going to slow our own development down,” they notched this up as a public perception win
This is them getting out in front of this and saying, “Hey, we want to be safe

We want to be responsible.” They’ve seen what’s happened with Meta and what’s happened with social media companies in the last two decades, and they are really cognizant of trying to get out in front of that

title: How Israel-Palestine broke up Sheeran-Macklemore
excerpt: Ed Sheeran (left) and Macklemore perform during the 2014 iHeartRadio Music Festival in Las Vegas, Nevada. | Kevin Winter/Getty Images This story appeared in&nbs
body: Ed Sheeran (left) and Macklemore perform during the 2014 iHeartRadio Music Festival in Las Vegas, Nevada. | Kevin Winter/Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here
I logged onto Slack this morning to find an incredible and indecipherable message from one of my coworkers

I briefly thought he was having a fever dream or I had forgotten how to read English. “Even some pro-Israel folks who hate Macklemore are ripshit at Robert Kraft for Streisand-effecting this guy,” the message read. …included were several links that eventually helped explain why “Macklemore,” “Robert Kraft” and “Israel” would ever appear in the same sentence
For those of you who have likewise not been following the fantastic implosion of Ed Sheeran’s ongoing tour, let’s break down this wild yarn

It begins with the washed-up millennial-cringe rapper Benjamin Hammond Haggerty, better known as Macklemore, who has lately a) taken up the cause of Palestinian independence and b) been opening for Sheeran on his blockbuster, 59-date Loop Tour.  Macklemore’s advocacy has not sat well with many observers, for reasons general (Gaza is one of the hottest buttons on earth) and particular (the rapper has a documented history of apparently antisemitic behavior , which he has since apologized for)

Last Friday, the artist Pink published a lengthy criticism of Macklemore’s on-stage polemic, writing that his comments and use of violent wartime imagery had frightened many Jewish people, including her

Around the same time, Robert Kraft — the sports magnate and Donald Trump ally who owns Gillette Stadium, outside of Boston — also allegedly notified Sheeran that he would not allow Macklemore to play his late-September show
Macklemore was subsequently dropped from the full tour.  Both he and Sheeran say multiple venues threatened to cancel if he continued to perform
And Kraft, who is Jewish, has also confirmed that he blocked Macklemore from playing at Gillette, citing both his recent advocacy and his “history of antisemitic rhetoric.”  But this is 2026
On Tuesday, the remaining opening acts and Sheeran’s backing band all pulled out of the tour in protest of the decision to boot Macklemore

Go a little deeper View Link The whole roiling mess has become a cipher of some of the biggest and most explosive topics in American culture and politics: the specter of antisemitism, the limits of free speech and “cancel culture,” and the stark generational differences in Americans’ views of Israel and Gaza.  It’s arguably no coincidence that this particular controversy erupted on the tour of two musicians who are iconic among the 30- to 45-year-old set

American millennials, as a generational and political cohort, have grown sharply more critical of the state of Israel in the past 10 years — laying the groundwork for Gen Z’s high-profile pro-Palestinian activism and driving a larger narrative shift in US politics.  This is, in some ways, an underappreciated dynamic in the debate over American support for Israel
Campus protests, organized by 20-something college students, have come to define young Americans’ growing disillusionment

Speaking on a podcast last year, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said “ there’s work to be done ” to win over Gen Z, in particular. (Macklemore, who is 43, named his pro-Palestinian protest song “Hind’s Hall” in honor of the protests at Columbia.)  But the attitudinal shift on Israel, especially on the left, began long before Gen Z became a major political force
Americans under 30 were, for instance, more likely to blame Israel than Hamas for the 2014 Gaza war
And during the mid-2010s, millennial activists sometimes wrapped Palestinian independence into broader social justice and anti-colonialist causes, including the Black Lives Matter movement
Several of the organizations that mobilized pro-Palestinian campus protests in 2024 had similarly been around for a decade or more
Today, of course, the shift extends beyond progressive millennials: Sympathy for Israel is down among younger Republicans , as well
It has, in fact, declined sharply across generations.  But over the past two years, the sharpest drop has been among Americans ages 35 to 54
In other words…the exact group of people who might still be jamming to Macklemore
One link for later ➨ Start your holiday planning now

But advance planning — in this case, incredibly advanced planning — can help you stick to a reasonable budget, reduce holiday stress, and ultimately yield a more meaningful, festive experience.  Before you go… Did you know… that there are more than 10,000 SpaceX satellites orbiting Earth? Proposals to put data centers in space would require so many additional satellites that stars would become less visible
